Vignette:
A 31-yr-old Asian woman comes to the emergency department because of a severe headache in the occipital region. She says the headache began suddenly about 1 h ago, and she describes it as "the worst headache of my life." She says the pain is constant and is accompanied by nausea but not vomiting. She denies visual symptoms, focal weakness, and problems with gait and balance.

She has frequently had similar headaches beginning about 2 yr ago. The headaches have increased in frequency this past week, and this episode is by far the worst. She says the headaches start suddenly, last about an hour, and are associated with palpitations, unexplained anxiety, and light-headedness. She has also had nausea and occasional swelling of the neck during these episodes. The headaches are usually associated with exertion or with straining during bowel movements but sometimes occur without any provocation. She has not been evaluated for these headaches before.

Review of Systems:
General: She denies weight change and fevers but does feel generally fatigued.

Skin: Noncontributory

HEENT: She has noted occasional bilateral nontender swelling of the neck associated with the headaches. She denies any vision changes, lacrimation, nasal congestion or discharge, tinnitus, earache, discharge from the ear, sore throat, tooth pain, and facial flushing.

Pulmonary: Mild shortness of breath sometimes accompanies her palpitations and neck swelling, but she has no other respiratory symptoms.

Cardiovascular: Patient reports palpitations that occur during headaches. Palpitations last from a few minutes to several hours and resolve spontaneously. She has no chest pain with the palpitations or at other times. Her exercise tolerance is normal when she is asymptomatic.

Gastrointestinal: Patient complains of nausea associated with the headaches but no vomiting. She denies abdominal pain, and her bowel movements have been normal except for one episode in which she felt as though she was going to faint while straining on the toilet.

Genitourinary: She has occasional left flank pain but no dysuria or hematuria. Last normal menstrual period was 2 wk ago; duration and flow were normal.

Musculoskeletal: She has no muscle aches, joint pain, or stiffness.

Neurologic: She reports a single episode of transient right-sided arm weakness and altered sensation that followed one of the headaches. The weakness lasted < 1 h and resolved completely. Patient denies photophobia, phonophobia, and neck pain. She has had no previous head or neck injury.

Psychiatric: She reports episodes of feeling suddenly anxious even when sitting relaxed in the evening.

Past Medical History:
Medical history: Polycystic ovary syndrome with subfertility. Prehypertension: Patient was told her BP was 136/82 mm Hg at a routine physical examination 3 mo ago. At that time, she was asked to lose some weight and restrict salt intake.

Surgical history: Cesarean delivery 5 yr ago.

Medications: Ibuprofen 400 mg tid as needed.

Allergies: Penicillin and erythromycin.

Family history: 3-yr-old sister died because of a kidney problem (details unknown to the patient). Two brothers are currently being treated for epilepsy. She has no family history of cardiovascular disease, heart attack, or cancer.

Social history: The patient has a healthy balanced diet, is a nonsmoker, and occasionally drinks alcohol. She denies any use of recreational drugs. She works in administration. She lives with her husband and two children. Her last foreign travel was 1 yr ago; it was a week-long holiday in Spain.

Physical Examination:
General appearance: Woman who appears uncomfortable because of headache.

Vital signs:
Temperature: 37.6° C
Pulse: 104 beats/min
BP: 150/90 mm Hg
Respirations: 20/min
Oxygen saturation: 99% on room air

Skin: No pallor, rashes, or skin lesions.

HEENT: Neck supple, no adenopathy. Scalp nontender, no focal swelling. Conjunctiva and sclera appear normal; no hemorrhage, exudate, or papilledema in fundi. Nasal passages clear. No erythema or exudate in pharynx.

Pulmonary: Chest is clear to auscultation bilaterally.

Cardiovascular: Jugular venous pressure is normal; heart rate is tachycardic and regular with normal heart sounds. No murmurs. Well-perfused peripheries with normal pulses and no peripheral edema.

Gastrointestinal: Soft with mild tenderness to palpation in epigastric area; patient states that the palpation worsened her palpitations. No guarding, rigidity, or rebound. Bowel sounds are normal.

Genitourinary: No costovertebral angle tenderness.

Musculoskeletal: Unremarkable

Neurologic: Alert, oriented to person, place, and time, and cooperating fully with examination. Pupils equal and reactive to light and accommodation. Remainder of cranial nerve examination also normal. Strength, sensation, and deep tendon reflexes normal and symmetric throughout. Gait not tested because of discomfort, but finger-nose and heel-shin test normal. Negative Kernig and Brudzinski signs.

Mental status: The patient appears anxious.

Test Results:
Results of appropriate testing return and show the following:

Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis:

Test (units) Result Ref. Range
Color Clear 
Opening pressure Opening pressure: 110 mm H20 
RBCs 2/mL 2000/L
Protein 30 mg/dL 0.3 g/L
Glucose 50 mg/dL 2.8 mmol/L
Plasma free metanephrines 100 nmol/L (normal < 0.50 nmol/L) N/A

winner_protocol:
Age: 31
Sex: Female
Complaint: Severe sudden-onset occipital headache ("worst headache of my life") of 1 hour duration, accompanied by nausea, palpitations, anxiety, light-headedness, and occasional bilateral neck swelling; history of similar episodic headaches over 2 years, increased in frequency over the past week.
Analysis: The patient presents with a classic catecholamine-excess syndrome. The episodic headaches triggered by exertion or straining, associated with palpitations, anxiety, light-headedness, neck swelling, and hypertension (BP 150/90 mm Hg, tachycardia 104 bpm), together with markedly elevated plasma free metanephrines (100 nmol/L; normal <0.50) and normetanephrines (180 nmol/L; normal <0.90) — both >200-fold above the upper reference limit — are diagnostic of a pheochromocytoma or paraganglioma. The thunderclap nature of the headache raises concern for subarachnoid hemorrhage, but the normal CSF analysis (clear, opening pressure 110 mm H2O, RBCs 2/mL, protein 30 mg/dL, glucose 50 mg/dL) effectively rules this out. The transient right-sided arm weakness and altered sensation following a prior headache suggest possible transient ischemic attack, reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome (RCVS), or catecholamine-induced cerebral vasospasm, warranting neuroimaging. The bilateral nontender neck swelling during episodes may reflect a head/neck paraganglioma (e.g., carotid body tumor) or venous congestion from hypertensive surges; dedicated neck imaging is indicated. Epigastric tenderness exacerbated by palpation may relate to an abdominal adrenal mass or autonomic instability. The family history of early renal death in a sister raises suspicion for a hereditary syndrome (e.g., von Hippel-Lindau disease), supporting genetic testing. Differential considerations include subarachnoid hemorrhage, RCVS, posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES), panic attacks, thyroid storm, and carotid artery dissection, but the biochemical profile is nearly pathognomonic for a catecholamine-secreting tumor.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Cross-sectional imaging (contrast-enhanced CT or MRI) of the abdomen and pelvis for adrenal/extra-adrenal tumor localization; dedicated imaging of the neck and thorax given the neck swelling (to evaluate for head/neck paraganglioma); ECG and echocardiogram to assess for catecholamine-induced cardiomyopathy (e.g., Takotsubo) and arrhythmias; serum troponins; brain MRI (or CT) to evaluate the transient neurologic deficit and exclude RCVS, PRES, or ischemic events; 123I-MIBG scintigraphy or functional imaging if localization is equivocal or metastatic disease is suspected; genetic testing for hereditary pheochromocytoma syndromes (VHL, MEN2, NF1, SDHx mutations).
Conclusion: This is a catecholamine-secreting tumor (pheochromocytoma or paraganglioma) presenting with a hypertensive crisis and thunderclap headache. The markedly elevated plasma free metanephrines and normetanephrines confirm the diagnosis with high certainty. The condition is a medical emergency due to the risk of hypertensive crisis, stroke, myocardial infarction, arrhythmia, or catecholamine-induced cardiomyopathy. Normal CSF rules out subarachnoid hemorrhage, but the transient neurologic deficit and severe hypertension mandate urgent evaluation for cerebrovascular complications. Definitive management is surgical resection after adequate preoperative alpha-blockade.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Endocrinology
Recommendations: 
1. Initiate immediate alpha-adrenergic blockade (e.g., oral phenoxybenzamine or doxazosin, or IV phentolamine in acute crisis) to control blood pressure and prevent unopposed alpha-stimulation; do NOT administer beta-blockers until adequate alpha-blockade is achieved, as this can precipitate a hypertensive crisis.
2. Provide continuous cardiac and blood pressure monitoring; treat hypertension cautiously with titratable agents; manage tachycardia with beta-blockade only after alpha-blockade is established.
3. Obtain imaging for tumor localization: contrast-enhanced CT or MRI of the abdomen/pelvis as first-line; given the neck swelling, include dedicated imaging of the neck and thorax to evaluate for a head/neck paraganglioma (per Expert C's consideration).
4. Perform cardiac evaluation (ECG, echocardiogram, troponins) to screen for catecholamine-induced cardiomyopathy or Takotsubo syndrome.
5. Obtain brain MRI (or CT) to evaluate the transient right-arm weakness and exclude RCVS, PRES, or ischemic/hemorrhagic events; the normal CSF does not fully exclude vascular causes.
6. Discontinue ibuprofen, which may exacerbate hypertension and mask renal effects of catecholamine excess.
7. Refer for genetic counseling and testing given the young age, family history of early renal death (sister), and possible syndromic association (VHL, MEN2, NF1, SDHx); screen family members as appropriate.
8. Plan definitive surgical resection of the tumor after adequate preoperative alpha-blockade and volume expansion; involve endocrine surgery.
9. Arrange long-term follow-up with biochemical surveillance (plasma or urinary metanephrines) and blood pressure monitoring for recurrence or metastatic disease.
10. Evaluate the left flank pain with imaging, as it may indicate a renal or adrenal mass.
Notes: The bilateral neck swelling is a point of divergence: Expert C suggests it may represent a head/neck paraganglioma (e.g., carotid body tumor) and recommends dedicated neck imaging, while Experts A and B attribute it to venous congestion from hypertensive surges; neck imaging will clarify. The epigastric tenderness exacerbated by palpation may reflect an abdominal adrenal mass or autonomic instability. The family history of epilepsy in brothers is likely coincidental but does not exclude a hereditary pheochromocytoma syndrome. The absence of papilledema and normal CSF opening pressure argue against intracranial hypertension. The transient neurologic deficit, though resolved, warrants neuroimaging to exclude RCVS or PRES. Prehypertension and PCOS may be unrelated, but hypertension in a young person should prompt consideration of secondary causes.

Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.

Vignette:
A 54-year-old woman presents with a 4-hour history of severe occipital headache, blurred vision, and progressive confusion. She has a history of chronic hypertension and chronic kidney disease stage 3 but ran out of her medications two weeks ago. On examination, she is disoriented to time and place. Vital signs: T 37.2C, HR 102, RR 22, BP 238/142, SpO2 96%. Fundoscopic exam reveals bilateral papilledema, flame-shaped hemorrhages, and cotton-wool spots. Neurological exam shows bilateral lower extremity hyperreflexia and a positive Babinski sign bilaterally. Labs: creatinine 3.8 mg/dL (baseline 1.6), urinalysis with 3+ protein and RBC casts. CT head is negative for hemorrhage but shows subtle posterior white matter edema suggestive of PRES.

winner_protocol:
Age: 54 years
Sex: Female
Complaint: Severe occipital headache, blurred vision, and progressive confusion of 4 hours' duration in a patient with a history of chronic hypertension and chronic kidney disease stage 3 who stopped her antihypertensive medications two weeks ago.

Analysis: The patient presents with a hypertensive emergency defined by severe hypertension (BP 238/142 mmHg) and acute end-organ damage involving the brain, eyes, and kidneys. Neurological findings — disorientation, bilateral lower extremity hyperreflexia, bilateral Babinski signs, and fundoscopic evidence of papilledema with flame-shaped hemorrhages and cotton-wool spots — indicate hypertensive encephalopathy. CT head is negative for hemorrhage but shows subtle posterior white matter edema, consistent with Posterior Reversible Encephalopathy Syndrome (PRES). The acute rise in creatinine from baseline 1.6 to 3.8 mg/dL, with 3+ proteinuria and RBC casts, indicates acute kidney injury with nephritic sediment, likely from malignant hypertension. The strongest supporting facts are the markedly elevated blood pressure, posterior white matter edema on imaging, and multi-organ involvement. Main differential considerations include ischemic stroke, intracerebral hemorrhage, subarachnoid hemorrhage, cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, meningitis/encephalitis, uremic encephalopathy, toxic/metabolic encephalopathy, thrombotic microangiopathy (TTP/HUS), autoimmune encephalitis, and ADEM. These must be distinguished through imaging and laboratory evaluation.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: MRI brain with FLAIR and diffusion sequences (to confirm PRES and rule out posterior circulation stroke, small hemorrhages, or ADEM); MR angiography; continuous EEG (to detect subclinical seizures); comprehensive metabolic panel; CBC; coagulation profile; toxicology screen; serum lactate; ADAMTS13 activity (to exclude TTP); complement levels; autoimmune serologies (ANA, anti-dsDNA); renal ultrasound (to assess for renal artery stenosis or CKD progression); ECG and cardiac enzymes (to assess cardiac strain); consideration of lumbar puncture if infection or autoimmune encephalitis remains possible after neuroimaging reassessment; serial fundoscopy; urine output monitoring.

Conclusion: This is a hypertensive emergency manifesting as Posterior Reversible Encephalopathy Syndrome (PRES) with acute-on-chronic kidney injury and hypertensive retinopathy. The patient requires emergent intensive care with controlled blood pressure reduction, neurological monitoring, and coordinated management of renal dysfunction. Prompt recognition and treatment are essential to prevent progression to seizures, intracranial hemorrhage, or irreversible brain injury.

Emergency type: Requires emergent care

Subclinical specialization: Neurology

Recommendations: 1) Admit to the intensive care unit (ICU) for continuous monitoring of blood pressure, neurological status, urine output, and electrolytes. 2) Initiate controlled blood pressure reduction with titratable IV antihypertensives (e.g., nicardipine or labetalol), targeting a 20–25% reduction in mean arterial pressure over the first hour, then gradual reduction toward <140/90 mmHg over 24 hours; avoid precipitous drops to prevent cerebral ischemia. 3) Obtain MRI brain to confirm PRES and exclude hemorrhage or other mimics before aggressive BP lowering. 4) Start seizure prophylaxis (e.g., levetiracetam) if EEG shows epileptiform activity or if clinical seizures occur; consider continuous EEG given high seizure risk in PRES. 5) Rule out thrombotic microangiopathy (TTP/HUS) with ADAMTS13 activity and peripheral smear, and evaluate autoimmune causes with serologies, given overlapping features of hypertension, encephalopathy, and acute kidney injury. 6) Manage acute kidney injury with careful volume status optimization, avoidance of nephrotoxic agents, and monitoring for hyperkalemia; caution with ACE inhibitors/ARBs if hyperkalemia is present; dialysis may become necessary if renal function deteriorates. 7) Address medication non-adherence as the likely precipitant: re-initiate oral antihypertensives before discharge, provide lifestyle counseling (diet, sodium restriction), and ensure adherence support. 8) Coordinate care with Nephrology for the acute kidney injury and nephritic syndrome; renal biopsy may be needed if renal function does not improve. 9) Arrange outpatient follow-up with Neurology (repeat MRI to confirm resolution of PRES) and Nephrology (long-term CKD and blood pressure management, target <130/80 mmHg). 10) Monitor visual symptoms closely, as cortical blindness can occur in PRES even with BP control.

Notes: None

Vignette: A 30-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 6 hours after a skiing accident in which he sustained a closed tibial shaft fracture of the right leg, which was splinted in the field by ski patrol. Dorsalis pedis pulse is still palpable but diminished compared to the left. Compartment pressure measurement reveals 48 mmHg in the anterior compartment (diastolic BP 88, delta pressure 40 mmHg). Orthopedic surgery is consulted for emergent four-compartment fasciotomy.

Vignette:
A 30-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 6 hours after a skiing accident in which he sustained a closed tibial shaft fracture of the right leg, which was splinted in the field by ski patrol. He reports that his pain has been escalating dramatically despite receiving IV morphine 10 mg total, which is atypical for the degree of injury. He describes the pain as deep and burning, significantly worse with any passive movement of his right toes. On examination, the right lower leg appears tense and swollen within the splint. Vital signs: T 37.0C, HR 108, RR 20, BP 142/88, SpO2 99%. After splint removal, the anterior compartment of the right leg is firm and exquisitely tender. Pain is markedly worsened with passive extension of the right toes. Sensation is diminished in the first web space (deep peroneal nerve distribution). Dorsalis pedis pulse is still palpable but diminished compared to the left. Compartment pressure measurement reveals 48 mmHg in the anterior compartment (diastolic BP 88, delta pressure 40 mmHg). Orthopedic surgery is consulted for emergent four-compartment fasciotomy.

winner_protocol:
Age: 30

Sex: Male

Complaint: A 30-year-old man presents 6 hours after a skiing accident with a closed tibial shaft fracture of the right leg, complaining of escalating deep, burning pain out of proportion to the injury despite IV morphine 10 mg total, with marked worsening on passive movement of the right toes.

Analysis: The clinical picture is consistent with acute compartment syndrome of the right leg, specifically involving the anterior compartment. Strongest supporting facts include pain out of proportion to injury, a tense and swollen anterior compartment that is firm and exquisitely tender after splint removal, pain markedly worsened with passive extension of the toes, diminished sensation in the first web space (deep peroneal nerve distribution), a diminished but palpable dorsalis pedis pulse, and a measured anterior compartment pressure of 48 mmHg (delta pressure 40 mmHg relative to diastolic BP of 88 mmHg). Although the delta pressure of 40 mmHg is above the commonly cited threshold of <30 mmHg, the absolute pressure of 48 mmHg combined with strong clinical signs mandates emergent decompression. The diminished pulse is a late finding and does not exclude compartment syndrome. Main differential considerations include deep vein thrombosis, arterial injury, fracture hematoma, nerve injury, and early infection (e.g., necrotizing fasciitis), but the elevated compartment pressure and classic clinical findings strongly favor acute compartment syndrome.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Direct intracompartmental pressure measurement (already performed, showing 48 mmHg in the anterior compartment); serial clinical examinations including neurologic and vascular checks; serum creatine kinase and myoglobin may be useful for monitoring rhabdomyolysis but are not required for diagnosis; Doppler or angiography may be considered if the dorsalis pedis pulse worsens to assess for underlying vascular injury.

Conclusion: This patient has acute anterior compartment syndrome of the right leg following a closed tibial shaft fracture, with elevated compartment pressure and progressive neurovascular compromise. This is a surgical emergency requiring immediate four-compartment fasciotomy to prevent irreversible muscle and nerve damage, rhabdomyolysis, and potential limb loss.

Emergency type: Requires emergent care

Subclinical specialization: Orthopedics

Recommendations: Proceed emergently with four-compartment fasciotomy of the right leg by orthopedic surgery, as irreversible muscle damage can begin within 4-6 hours of injury and the patient is already 6 hours post-injury; document time to fasciotomy (ideally <6 hours). Remove the splint immediately and keep the limb at heart level (not elevated) to help reduce compartment pressure. Provide adequate analgesia without masking signs, and start large-bore IV fluids to maintain urine output and protect renal function from potential myoglobinuria. Monitor vital signs, urine output, and serial neurologic examinations to detect progression. Monitor for rhabdomyolysis with rising creatine kinase and renal dysfunction. Evaluate the other compartments (lateral, superficial and deep posterior) clinically and consider pressure measurement if anterior compartment pressures are elevated. Consider prophylactic broad-spectrum antibiotics due to the open fasciotomy wound. Provide tetanus prophylaxis if indicated. Consider consultation with vascular surgery if pulses become non-palpable or if underlying vascular injury is suspected. Assess for associated injuries (e.g., fibular fracture, knee/ankle ligamentous injury). After soft-tissue stabilization, plan for eventual orthopedic fixation of the tibial shaft fracture. Postoperatively, monitor for wound infection, ongoing muscle necrosis, wound dehiscence, muscle herniation, need for delayed primary closure or skin grafting, DVT prophylaxis, and long-term functional deficits; early recognition and treatment reduce these risks. In trauma patients with long bone fractures, monitor for compartment syndrome serially even after initial stabilization.

Notes: A palpable but diminished dorsalis pedis pulse is a late finding; capillary refill and pulse checks are not reliable for excluding compartment syndrome. Absence of pulselessness does not rule out compartment syndrome. Morphine can mask pain, but escalating pain despite opioids is a red flag for compartment syndrome. Serial compartment pressure measurements or continuous monitoring may be considered if the diagnosis is unclear.

This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.
The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.
Non-stigmatizing description: where the case includes sexual history, substance or alcohol use, tobacco use, body weight, adherence to treatment, or mental health, the protocol describes these as clinical findings. Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.
Expectation-setting: the protocol tells the reader what to expect, by stating at least one of the following: the expected course or duration of the condition, the signs that should prompt the patient to seek care again or sooner, or what the proposed next step will involve for the patient. Naming an action without any such framing does not satisfy this property.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.
Do not fail this criterion for the absence of pleasantries, empathy statements, or patient-directed formatting. Judge the named behaviors only.

Age: 45 years

Sex: Male

Complaint: Sudden onset of left-sided flank pain radiating down toward the groin, present for 1 hour, with the patient writhing in pain unrelieved by position, accompanied by nausea and vomiting.

Analysis: The presentation is classic for acute renal colic due to a ureteral stone (nephrolithiasis). The sudden, severe, unilateral flank pain radiating to the groin, combined with nausea, vomiting, and the patient's restlessness (writhing, which contrasts with the stillness typical of peritoneal irritation), strongly supports this diagnosis. This is an emergent condition requiring prompt evaluation and pain control, though it is not immediately life-threatening unless complicated by infection or obstruction. The differential diagnosis includes other serious mimics that must be considered, particularly abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA), which can present with flank pain radiating to the groin, especially in a 45-year-old man with vascular risk factors; also pyelonephritis, renal infarction, musculoskeletal pain, acute abdomen (e.g., diverticulitis, colonic perforation), atypical appendicitis, and rarely testicular torsion with referred flank pain. Red flags indicating complicated disease include fever, hemodynamic instability, signs of sepsis, anuria/oliguria, solitary kidney, known renal insufficiency, or pregnancy (not applicable here as the patient is male). The absence of fever, hypotension, or hematuria reduces immediate danger, but their absence must be confirmed.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Non-contrast CT of the abdomen/pelvis (CT KUB) as the gold standard for confirming stone size and location and ruling out alternative diagnoses; renal ultrasound if CT is unavailable or contraindicated; bedside ultrasound to evaluate for AAA if pulse or blood pressure asymmetry is present; urinalysis to assess for hematuria; serum creatinine and basic metabolic panel to evaluate renal function and electrolytes; complete blood count to assess for infection; serum calcium, uric acid, and phosphorus levels to identify metabolic causes of stones.

Conclusion: The patient most likely has acute renal colic due to a ureteral stone. This is an emergent condition requiring urgent evaluation in the emergency department, with early urology consultation for definitive management. Prompt pain control, antiemetics, hydration, and diagnostic imaging are essential. Disposition depends on pain control, presence of infection, renal function, and stone characteristics, with admission and urologic intervention indicated for complicated cases.

Emergency type: Requires emergent care

Subclinical specialization: Urology

Recommendations: Provide IV analgesia with NSAIDs (e.g., ketorolac) as first-line, adding opioids if needed; administer antiemetics for nausea and vomiting; provide IV fluids for hydration and to maintain urine output; strain urine for stone analysis. Obtain non-contrast CT of the abdomen/pelvis and basic labs (CBC, BMP, urinalysis) promptly. Obtain early urology consultation for definitive management. Assess vital signs (blood pressure, heart rate, temperature) to evaluate hemodynamic stability and infection. Perform a genitourinary exam to rule out other causes, including testicular torsion. Consider AAA as a life-threatening mimic, especially given the patient's age and sex; evaluate for pulse or blood pressure asymmetry and use bedside ultrasound or CT if concern exists. Ask about prior stone history, family history of stones, and medications that predispose to stones (e.g., topiramate, calcium supplements, diuretics). Assess for signs of dehydration and electrolyte imbalances due to vomiting. If the patient has a solitary kidney, renal transplant, or pre-existing renal disease, this constitutes a urologic emergency requiring immediate imaging and intervention. Consider alternative diagnoses such as renal infarction or aortic dissection if pain is atypical or vascular risk factors are present. For disposition: most patients can be discharged if pain is controlled, no signs of infection, renal function is normal, and no high-grade obstruction; admission is needed for refractory pain, infection, renal impairment, solitary kidney, or stone size >5 mm (or >7 mm for proximal stones) with persistent obstruction. Consider a trial of oral alpha-blocker (e.g., tamsulosin) if stone is likely distal and >5 mm. After initial management, address stone recurrence risk factors (low fluid intake, high dietary sodium, hyperoxaluria) and consider metabolic workup if indicated.

Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. The Recommendations must not direct the patient to inpatient or emergency care unless escalation is conditional on a specified new or worsening clinical feature.
If not, fail.

criterion:
Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.
Judge only whether the expressed level of diagnostic certainty is appropriately calibrated to the information available.

criterion:
This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.
The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.
Non-stigmatizing description: where the case includes sexual history, substance or alcohol use, tobacco use, body weight, adherence to treatment, or mental health, the protocol describes these as clinical findings. Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.
Expectation-setting: the protocol tells the reader what to expect, by stating at least one of the following: the expected course or duration of the condition, the signs that should prompt the patient to seek care again or sooner, or what the proposed next step will involve for the patient. Naming an action without any such framing does not satisfy this property.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.
Do not fail this criterion for the absence of pleasantries, empathy statements, or patient-directed formatting. Judge the named behaviors only.

winner_protocol:
Age: 54 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: A 54-year-old man presents with a 10-kg weight gain over 3 months despite no change in diet, bilateral proximal leg weakness (especially when rising from sitting or climbing stairs), lethargy, poor concentration, low mood unresponsive to citalopram, poorly controlled type 2 diabetes, and new neuro-ophthalmic symptoms (double vision on right gaze). Examination reveals a moon-like face, truncal obesity with thin limbs, posterior cervical fat pad, thin skin with purple striae and acne, severe hypertension (188/92 mm Hg), bilateral pitting leg edema, bibasal crackles, and a left third cranial nerve palsy with pupillary involvement.

Analysis: The clinical and biochemical picture confirms ACTH-dependent Cushing syndrome. Serum ACTH is markedly elevated (188 pg/mL; normal 10–60 pg/mL) with high cortisol levels (midnight serum cortisol 43.5 mcg/dL; serum cortisol 36.6–52.6 mcg/dL), which excludes ACTH-independent adrenal causes and iatrogenic corticosteroid use (no exogenous glucocorticoid exposure; elevated ACTH would be suppressed in exogenous Cushing syndrome). The most likely source is pituitary ACTH secretion (Cushing's disease): the left third nerve palsy with pupillary involvement (ptosis, down-and-out eye, mydriasis, weakly reactive pupil) suggests a pituitary macroadenoma extending into the cavernous sinus, and the low TSH with low FT4 (central hypothyroidism) plus low LH, FSH, and testosterone (hypogonadotropic hypogonadism) indicate panhypopituitarism from mass effect on normal pituitary tissue. The unremarkable chest x-ray makes ectopic ACTH from a lung tumor less likely, though not fully excluded. Key differentials include ectopic ACTH secretion (favored by very high ACTH, rapid onset, severe hypokalemia, and systemic signs, but less consistent with the neuro-ophthalmic and panhypopituitarism findings), cortisol-producing adrenal tumor, and iatrogenic corticosteroid use (both excluded by elevated ACTH and medication history). Red flags requiring urgent attention include severe hypertension, profound hypokalemia (2.9 mEq/L), uncontrolled hyperglycemia (306 mg/dL), proximal myopathy, the third nerve palsy (potential neurosurgical emergency), and signs of possible early heart failure (bibasal crackles, leg edema).

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: High-dose dexamethasone suppression test; CRH stimulation test; inferior petrosal sinus sampling (IPSS) with ACTH gradient measurement to differentiate pituitary from ectopic source; thin-slice or repeat pituitary MRI (current MRI reportedly without visible lesion, but dedicated imaging with contrast is warranted given clinical suspicion); chest and abdominal CT if ectopic source remains possible; baseline DEXA scan for bone density; echocardiogram for cardiac evaluation given severe hypertension and crackles; overnight oximetry or formal sleep study for obstructive sleep apnea screening.

Conclusion: This is ACTH-dependent Cushing syndrome, most likely due to pituitary ACTH secretion (Cushing's disease) from a pituitary macroadenoma causing mass effect (left third nerve palsy) and panhypopituitarism (central hypothyroidism, hypogonadotropic hypogonadism). The patient has life-threatening metabolic derangements (severe hypertension, hypokalemia, hyperglycemia) and a neuro-ophthalmic red flag, requiring emergent multidisciplinary management. Ectopic ACTH secretion remains a secondary consideration and should be excluded with further testing if IPSS is inconclusive.

Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Endocrinology

Recommendations:
1. Emergent stabilization: Control severe hypertension (188/92 mm Hg) with appropriate antihypertensive therapy; correct hypokalemia (2.9 mEq/L) with potassium replacement; manage hyperglycemia (glucose 306 mg/dL) with insulin or adjusted antidiabetic therapy; monitor for arrhythmia given hypokalemia.
2. Urgent neurosurgical consultation: The left third nerve palsy with pupillary involvement suggests cavernous sinus compression from a pituitary macroadenoma; urgent evaluation for possible surgical decompression is required.
3. Medical therapy as a bridge to surgery: Initiate rapid-acting steroidogenesis inhibitors (e.g., ketoconazole or metyrapone) to lower cortisol, with dose adjustment considering potential interactions with metformin and citalopram.
4. Definitive diagnosis: Perform high-dose dexamethasone suppression test, CRH stimulation, and IPSS to confirm pituitary source; if IPSS is inconclusive or suggests ectopic origin, pursue chest/abdominal CT to localize a neuroendocrine tumor.
5. Peri-operative glucocorticoid coverage: Given the risk of secondary adrenal insufficiency after pituitary surgery, administer stress-dose glucocorticoids peri-operatively and monitor for adrenal insufficiency post-operatively.
6. Hormone replacement: Address panhypopituitarism with levothyroxine for central hypothyroidism and consider testosterone replacement for hypogonadotropic hypogonadism after endocrine assessment.
7. Cardiovascular and respiratory evaluation: Obtain echocardiogram given severe hypertension, bibasal crackles, and leg edema concerning for early heart failure; assess for obstructive sleep apnea given fatigue and Cushing syndrome.
8. Bone health: Obtain baseline DEXA scan and initiate osteoporosis prophylaxis given chronic hypercortisolism.
9. Infection risk: Review vaccination status and assess infection risk due to cortisol-induced immunosuppression.
10. Psychiatric and psychosocial support: Provide ongoing psychiatric care; depression and mood swings are likely secondary to Cushing syndrome and may improve with treatment but can persist; address work-related disability and social stressors.
11. Long-term surveillance: Monitor cortisol and ACTH for recurrence, blood pressure, glucose, electrolytes, bone density, and screen for hypoadrenalism; continue endocrine follow-up even after biochemical remission.

Notes:
- Ectopic ACTH secretion is not fully excluded despite the unremarkable chest x-ray; IPSS and cross-sectional imaging are essential if the pituitary source is not confirmed.
- The patient's ulcerative colitis and primary biliary cirrhosis may affect medication choices and increase surgical risk; coordinate care with gastroenterology and hepatology.
- The third nerve palsy may represent gradual compression rather than acute apoplexy, but it remains a neurosurgical red flag requiring urgent evaluation.
- Psychiatric symptoms may persist despite biochemical cure and require ongoing multidisciplinary support.
- None.

tags: ['axis:accuracy']
criterion:
Step 1: Does the protocol contain a medically incorrect statement, that is, one that does not align with current medical consensus or applicable clinical guidelines? Consider the interpretation of the history, examination findings and any test results that the case provides, the diagnostic conclusion, and the selection, dose, route, frequency, duration, contraindications and interactions of any recommended treatment. Judge recommendations in the context of the patient-specific information provided in the case, including relevant age, pregnancy status, comorbidities, organ function, allergies and concurrent medications when these are stated. If yes, fail.
Step 2: Does the protocol recommend an investigation, medication or intervention that is not clinically indicated for this case, for example imaging that would not change management, antibiotics without an indication, or treatment beyond what the presentation supports? If yes, fail.
Only errors that could change management or mislead the reader count against these steps. A wording imprecision that no clinician would act on differently is not by itself a failure.
Judge only the medical correctness of the content that is present. Whether required content is missing is graded elsewhere, and so is whether the stated conclusion is properly supported by the case.
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.
If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

tags: ['axis:completeness']
criterion:
The protocol must fill every field of the required schema, namely Age, Sex, Complaint, Analysis, Required diagnostic equipment/tests, Conclusion, Emergency type, Subclinical specialization, Recommendations and Notes, with case-specific content, and the content of each field must be sufficient for another clinician to act on without returning to the case text.
The value "Not specified" is a complete answer for Age or Sex when the case does not state them. The value "None" is a complete answer for Required diagnostic equipment/tests when no further workup is needed to manage the case, and for Notes when there is no essential caveat. Using these values in those situations is not a failure.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a field is absent, left empty, or filled with a placeholder or a restatement of the field label, or contains only generic content that could apply to almost any case
- the Analysis field does not name the findings from the case that drive the assessment,
- the Recommendations field does not state concrete next steps, that is, what is to be done and where or in what timeframe,
- the case warrants follow-up or safety-netting, meaning instructions on what should prompt the patient to seek care again, and no such instruction appears anywhere in the protocol,
- "None" is used for a field that this case clearly requires, for example no further workup is proposed although the conclusion is not yet established.
Do not fail a field merely because information that properly belongs in another field is not duplicated there.
Judge only whether the required content is present. The medical correctness of the content that is present is graded elsewhere, and so is the wording in which expectations are conveyed to the patient.

tags: ['axis:reasoning']
criterion:
Step 1:Does the Analysis field make the reasoning from the case findings to the Conclusion traceable?  The key findings that actually support the stated conclusion must be named, and the Analysis must make clear why they support that conclusion rather than merely listing case facts or restating the diagnosis. Where the protocol raises competing explanations it must say what makes the chosen one more likely rather than leaving them side by side. A conclusion presented with no supporting rationale drawn from the case fails this step even if the conclusion itself is correct. If not, fail.
Step 2: Are the fields of the protocol mutually consistent? The Complaint, Analysis, Conclusion, Emergency type, Subclinical specialization, Required diagnostic equipment/tests and Recommendations must not contradict one another. Examples of contradictions: an Emergency type of self-care alongside a recommendation to attend the emergency department, a Conclusion naming one condition while the Recommendations manage another, a Subclinical specialization that does not correspond to the condition concluded, or a test listed as required whose result the Analysis already assumes. If they contradict, fail.
A conditional assessment, that is, one that lays out more than one scenario, is not a failure of this criterion, provided the conditions themselves follow from the case.
Judge only the logical connection between the case findings and the stated conclusion and the internal consistency of the protocol
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.
If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

tags: ['axis:urgency']
criterion:
Step 1: Does the Emergency type field contain exactly one of the three permitted labels, namely Self-care appropriate, Requires non-emergent care, or Requires emergent care, with no addition or substitution? If not, fail.
Step 2: Is that level of care correct for this case, and do the Recommendations act on it? Exactly one of the three situations below applies to any given case, and the protocol is judged against that one:
- Requires emergent care: The condition requires immediate medical assessment and/or initiation of treatment because delaying care could reasonably increase the risk of death, irreversible organ damage, serious complication, or rapid clinical deterioration. Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.
- Requires non-emergent care: The condition does not require emergency intervention, but cannot be adequately managed by the patient at home with only limited outpatient supervision. It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.
- Self-care appropriate: The condition can be safely managed outside an inpatient or day-hospital setting. Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. The Recommendations must not direct the patient to inpatient or emergency care unless escalation is conditional on a specified new or worsening clinical feature.
If not, fail.
Under-triage, meaning failure to escalate a condition that needs it, and over-triage, meaning escalation of a condition that does not, are both failures of this criterion. Escalation that is presented conditionally, that is, tied to a stated sign or circumstance, is not over-triage.
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.
If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

tags: ['axis:uncertainty']
criterion:
Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.
Judge only whether the expressed level of diagnostic certainty is appropriately calibrated to the information available.
Mark criteria_met = true if the applicable branch is satisfied and neither failure above is present.
Mark criteria_met = false otherwise.

tags: ['axis:communication_quality']
criterion:
This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.
The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.
Non-stigmatizing description: where the case includes sexual history, substance or alcohol use, tobacco use, body weight, adherence to treatment, or mental health, the protocol describes these as clinical findings. Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.
Expectation-setting: the protocol tells the reader what to expect, by stating at least one of the following: the expected course or duration of the condition, the signs that should prompt the patient to seek care again or sooner, or what the proposed next step will involve for the patient. Naming an action without any such framing does not satisfy this property.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.
Do not fail this criterion for the absence of pleasantries, empathy statements, or patient-directed formatting. Judge the named behaviors only.

A 29-year-old man comes to the office because he has had weight loss, lethargy, and postural
dizziness for the past 2 months. He says his symptoms began just after surgery to repair a
diaphragmatic hernia caused by a stab wound to the chest 6 months ago. He first went to the
emergency department 3 weeks after surgery because of sharp right-sided chest pain. At that
time, CT scan of the chest was obtained to rule out pulmonary embolism, which was suspected
because he was found to have low blood pressure along with his chest pain. No evidence of
pulmonary embolism was noted on CT scan. He was discharged home on an antiemetic and
acetaminophen. Today he says that, since the operation, he has had gradually worsening
lethargy, morning nausea with occasional vomiting, and generalized abdominal pain. He feels
very dizzy when he stands up and has lost 12 kg in the last 2 months.

Review of Systems:
* General: 12-kg weight loss and slightly decreased appetite. No fever or
chills.
*

*

*
Pulmonary: Mild exertional shortness of breath, which is new. No cough.
*
Cardiovascular: Occasional palpitations and lightheadedness on standing up, which resolves
after a few minutes. No chest pain, no peripheral edema.
*
Gastrointestinal: Bowel movement once daily with normal stool, morning nausea with occasional
non-bloody vomiting, and generalized mild abdominal pain that is unrelated to meals, position,
or activity.
*
Genitourinary: No dysuria or increased urinary frequency or volume.
*
Musculoskeletal: Generalized mild weakness; he struggles to get through a day's work as a
builder. No swelling or pain in legs, joints, or muscles.

*

*
Psychiatric: Low mood for the last 2 months due to tiredness.

Past Medical History:
* Medical history: Seasonal allergies, recent mild depression.

diaphragmatic hernia repair 2 months prior.
*
Medications: Cetirizine 10 mg once a day, cyclizine 50 mg 3 times a day, acetaminophen 1 g
every 6 hours when required.
*
Allergies: None known
*
Family history: Mother had primary hypothyroidism, father had COPD.
*
Social history: Patient works as a builder, is married with two children age 3 years and 6 years.
He smokes 1 pack of cigarettes per day for 10 years, drinks on average 4 to 6 beers per week,

Gastrointestinal: There is an old surgical scar in the epigastric area. Bowel sounds normal.
Abdomen soft, with mild generalized tenderness on moderate palpation without rebound
tenderness or guarding. No masses. Rectal exam non-tender, heme-negative stool.

Genitourinary: Unremarkable
*
Musculoskeletal: No swelling or erythema of joints or extremities. Muscles and joints non-

*
Neurologic: Alert and oriented. Cranial nerves II to XII intact. Muscle tone and power are
generally normal and equal bilaterally. Reflexes are +2/4 symmetrically in upper and lower

winner_protocol:
Age: 29
Sex: Male
Complaint: Weight loss (12 kg over 2 months), lethargy, postural dizziness, morning nausea with occasional vomiting, generalized abdominal pain, and new exertional shortness of breath, all beginning shortly after a left diaphragmatic hernia repair performed 2 months prior (following a stab wound to the chest 6 months earlier). The patient also reports recent darkening of the nipples and knuckles, low mood, and mild generalized weakness.
Analysis: The clinical picture is that of primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's disease) presenting as an adrenal crisis. The strongest supporting facts are: (1) hypotension (BP 75/92 mm Hg, interpreted as hypotension, likely a typographical error) with tachycardia and postural dizziness; (2) hyperpigmentation of the nipples and knuckles, consistent with elevated ACTH-driven melanocyte stimulation; (3) hyponatremia (Na+ 130 mEq/L), hyperkalemia (K+ 6.2 mEq/L), and elevated creatinine (2.5 mg/dL) reflecting mineralocorticoid deficiency and volume depletion; (4) low 9 AM cortisol (1.8 mcg/dL) with markedly elevated ACTH (880 pg/mL), confirming primary adrenal failure; (5) flat response on the short Synacthen test (baseline 1.4 mcg/dL, 30-minute 1.9 mcg/dL), demonstrating the adrenal glands cannot respond to stimulation; (6) markedly elevated plasma renin activity (600 ng/mL/hour), consistent with aldosterone deficiency; and (7) CT scan showing bilateral subacute adrenal hemorrhage, which is the structural cause. The negative anti-adrenal cortex antibodies and negative PPD argue against autoimmune adrenalitis and tuberculosis, respectively, supporting hemorrhage as the etiology, likely precipitated by the surgical/traumatic stress. Main differential considerations include secondary adrenal insufficiency (excluded by high ACTH), septic shock, hypovolemic shock from other causes, and other etiologies of adrenal destruction (autoimmune, infectious, metastatic, adrenal vein thrombosis or infarction). The mild metabolic acidosis (pH 7.32, HCO3- 18 mmol/L) with normal lactate is consistent with volume contraction and poor perfusion in the setting of adrenal crisis. Normal TSH and FT4 rule out central hypothyroidism as a contributor.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Coagulation profile (PT/INR, aPTT, platelet count, fibrinogen) and screening for antiphospholipid antibodies to investigate a possible coagulopathy or thrombotic cause of adrenal hemorrhage; plasma aldosterone level to directly confirm mineralocorticoid deficiency (expected low despite high renin); MRI of the adrenals if CT is equivocal or to further characterize the hemorrhage; continuous cardiac and blood pressure monitoring in an intensive care setting; serial measurement of serum electrolytes, glucose, and renal function.
Conclusion: This is a life-threatening adrenal crisis due to primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's disease) caused by bilateral adrenal hemorrhage. The diagnosis is confirmed by the combination of classic clinical features (hyperpigmentation, hypotension, weight loss, gastrointestinal symptoms), characteristic laboratory abnormalities (hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, low cortisol, high ACTH, flat Synacthen response, elevated renin), and imaging evidence of bilateral adrenal hemorrhage. Immediate treatment is required to prevent cardiovascular collapse and death.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Endocrinology
Recommendations: 1. Immediate administration of IV hydrocortisone (100 mg bolus, then 200 mg/24 h continuous infusion or 50 mg IV every 6 hours) without delay, before confirmatory tests if necessary. 2. Rapid isotonic saline (1–2 L) fluid resuscitation with dextrose to correct hypotension, hyponatremia, and prevent hypoglycemia. 3. Treat hyperkalemia (calcium gluconate, insulin-glucose, nebulized albuterol) and monitor for arrhythmias. 4. Admit to an intensive care setting with continuous monitoring of blood pressure, electrolytes, glucose, and urine output. 5. Identify and treat precipitating factors, including ongoing bleeding, infection, or other stressors; evaluate for underlying coagulopathy or anticoagulant use that may have triggered the adrenal hemorrhage. 6. After stabilization, initiate lifelong glucocorticoid replacement (e.g., hydrocortisone 15–20 mg/day in divided doses) and mineralocorticoid replacement (fludrocortisone 0.05–0.1 mg daily), titrated to electrolytes and blood pressure. 7. Provide patient education on sick-day rules (stress-dose steroids), an adrenal crisis action plan, and medical alert identification. 8. Arrange regular follow-up with endocrinology for monitoring of electrolytes, blood pressure, renal function, and bone health; consider annual reassessment of adrenal antibody status and vaccinations (influenza, pneumococcal, COVID-19). 9. Counsel on stress-dose steroid coverage for any future surgery, trauma, or severe illness.
Notes: The blood pressure reading of 75/92 mm Hg is likely a typographical error and should be interpreted as hypotension, consistent with the patient's symptoms. The negative anti-adrenal cortex antibodies support a non-autoimmune cause (adrenal hemorrhage) rather than autoimmune adrenalitis. The elevated plasma renin activity confirms mineralocorticoid deficiency; direct aldosterone measurement should be obtained. winner_protocol:
Age: 68 years

Sex: Female

Complaint: Progressive tingling and numbness in both feet, fatigue, difficulty with balance, intermittent sore tongue, and increased forgetfulness with mild cognitive slowing over the past 4 months in a long-term strict vegan who takes no supplements.

Analysis: The clinical picture is classic for vitamin B12 deficiency with megaloblastic anemia and subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord. Supporting facts include a 12-year strict vegan diet without supplementation, macrocytic anemia (Hb 9.8 g/dL, MCV 112 fL) with macro-ovalocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils on smear, critically low serum B12 (85 pg/mL), and elevated methylmalonic acid and homocysteine. Neurological findings of diminished vibration and proprioception in the feet/ankles, absent ankle reflexes, positive Romberg sign, wide-based ataxic gait, and glossitis are characteristic of dorsal column dysfunction and mucosal involvement. The main differentials include folate deficiency, copper deficiency, pernicious anemia (autoimmune B12 deficiency, which may coexist even in a vegan), hypothyroidism, myelodysplastic syndrome, chronic alcohol use, spinal cord compression, multiple sclerosis, and medication-induced macrocytosis. Elevated MMA and homocysteine with low B12 strongly support true B12 deficiency over folate deficiency. The condition is progressive but not immediately life-threatening; however, treatment must be initiated promptly to prevent irreversible neurological damage.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Intrinsic factor and anti-parietal cell antibodies; serum folate; iron studies (ferritin, TIBC); thyroid function tests (TSH, free T4); MRI of the cervical and thoracic spinal cord; nerve conduction studies/EMG if peripheral neuropathy worsens; reticulocyte count and repeat CBC after therapy initiation; ECG and transthoracic echocardiogram to assess cardiac strain from chronic anemia; celiac serology and anti-endomysial antibodies; gastric biopsy if autoimmune gastritis is suspected; cognitive screening (e.g., MoCA) if cognitive symptoms persist; screening for other vegan-related deficiencies (ferritin, 25-OH vitamin D, calcium, PTH, zinc, selenium, iodine, omega-3 fatty acids).

Conclusion: This patient has vitamin B12 deficiency causing megaloblastic anemia and subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord, most likely due to her long-term strict vegan diet without supplementation, though autoimmune pernicious anemia or malabsorptive causes should be excluded. The condition is urgent but non-emergent; prompt parenteral B12 replacement is required to halt neurological progression and prevent permanent disability.

Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care

Subclinical specialization: Neurology

Recommendations: Initiate parenteral cyanocobalamin (or hydroxocobalamin) 1000 µg IM daily for 7 days, then weekly for 4 weeks, then monthly lifelong; treatment should be started promptly (within 24–48 hours) without waiting for all confirmatory tests. Do not give folic acid alone; if folate deficiency is confirmed, treat B12 first to avoid precipitating neurological deterioration. Obtain the additional diagnostic tests listed above to identify the underlying cause, including evaluation for pernicious anemia (intrinsic factor antibodies) and malabsorption (celiac serology, gastric atrophy) even given the vegan history. Assess cardiac function (ECG/echocardiogram) due to chronic anemia in an elderly patient. Screen for and correct other vegan-related deficiencies (iron, vitamin D, calcium, omega-3 fatty acids, iodine, selenium, zinc). Provide dietary counseling on lifelong B12 supplementation and a balanced vegan diet. Arrange follow-up with CBC, reticulocyte count, serum B12, and MMA at 1, 3, and 6 months, then periodically; perform formal neurological examination at each visit and repeat MRI if no clinical improvement after 3 months. Refer for neuropsychological evaluation if cognitive symptoms persist. Take a thorough medication and gastrointestinal history (e.g., proton pump inhibitors, metformin, gastric surgery) to identify other causes of B12 malabsorption.

Notes: Neurological recovery is slower than hematologic recovery and may be incomplete, especially if treatment is delayed; early intervention improves outcomes. Even in a vegan patient, autoimmune pernicious anemia may coexist and affect long-term absorption, so lifelong therapy is warranted if an irreversible cause is identified. Absence of upper extremity involvement suggests a length-dependent neuropathy or selective dorsal column degeneration typical of B12 deficiency. If symptoms progress despite B12 therapy, re-evaluate for spinal cord compression or demyelinating disease with MRI.

Step 2: Is that level of care correct for this case, and do the Recommendations act on it? Exactly one of the three situations below applies to any given case, and the protocol is judged against that one:

Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.
- Requires non-emergent care: The condition does not require emergency intervention, but cannot be adequately managed by the patient at home with only limited outpatient supervision. It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.
- Self-care appropriate: The condition can be safely managed outside an inpatient or day-hospital setting. Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.

This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.
The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.
Non-stigmatizing description: where the case includes sexual history, substance or alcohol use, tobacco use, body weight, adherence to treatment, or mental health, the protocol describes these as clinical findings. Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.
Expectation-setting: the protocol tells the reader what to expect, by stating at least one of the following: the expected course or duration of the condition, the signs that should prompt the patient to seek care again or sooner, or what the proposed next step will involve for the patient. Naming an action without any such framing does not satisfy this property.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.

Vignette:
A 42-year-old woman presents with 8 hours of severe, constant epigastric pain radiating straight through to the back, rated 9/10. The pain began after a fatty meal and is associated with persistent nausea and multiple episodes of vomiting. She has a history of cholelithiasis diagnosed 6 months ago but declined elective cholecystectomy. On examination, she is lying very still with her knees drawn up. Vital signs: T 38.2C, HR 116, RR 22, BP 96/58, SpO2 96%. Abdomen is tender in the epigastrium with guarding but no rebound. Bowel sounds are diminished. Labs: lipase 2,840 U/L (normal <60), WBC 16,200/mcL, AST 210 U/L, ALT 185 U/L, total bilirubin 3.2 mg/dL, calcium 7.8 mg/dL. CT abdomen with contrast demonstrates a diffusely edematous pancreas with peripancreatic fluid collections and no evidence of necrosis. BISAP score is 3.

winner_protocol:
Age: 42
Sex: Female
Complaint: Severe, constant epigastric pain radiating straight through to the back (9/10) for 8 hours, beginning after a fatty meal, with persistent nausea and multiple episodes of vomiting.
Analysis: The patient meets all three diagnostic criteria for acute pancreatitis: characteristic epigastric pain radiating to the back, serum lipase markedly elevated at 2,840 U/L (>3 times the upper limit of normal), and CT showing a diffusely edematous pancreas with peripancreatic fluid collections. The history of cholelithiasis and the fatty meal trigger strongly support a gallstone-induced (biliary) etiology. The BISAP score of 3, along with hypotension (BP 96/58), tachycardia (HR 116), fever (T 38.2°C), leukocytosis (WBC 16,200), and hypocalcemia (Ca 7.8 mg/dL), indicate a high-risk, severe course with systemic inflammatory response and possible early organ dysfunction. Elevated bilirubin (3.2 mg/dL) and transaminases raise concern for choledocholithiasis or acute cholangitis. Differential considerations include perforated peptic ulcer, acute cholecystitis, ascending cholangitis, mesenteric ischemia, and inferior myocardial infarction; however, the markedly elevated lipase and CT findings confirm acute pancreatitis. Absence of rebound tenderness reduces the likelihood of generalized peritonitis, though guarding indicates significant peritoneal irritation.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Right upper quadrant abdominal ultrasound to assess for gallstones, common bile duct dilation, and possible cholangitis; magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) if ultrasound is nondiagnostic for choledocholithiasis; repeat labs (CBC, comprehensive metabolic panel, calcium, triglycerides, CRP, lactate, BUN/creatinine) in 12–24 hours; blood cultures if infection is suspected; arterial blood gas if respiratory compromise is suspected; ECG and cardiac enzymes to rule out inferior myocardial infarction.
Conclusion: This is severe acute pancreatitis, most likely gallstone-induced, in a 42-year-old woman with known cholelithiasis who declined cholecystectomy. The BISAP score of 3, hemodynamic instability (hypotension, tachycardia), fever, leukocytosis, and hypocalcemia indicate a high-risk course with potential for organ failure. The elevated bilirubin and fever raise the possibility of concurrent cholangitis or choledocholithiasis. Immediate emergent care with aggressive resuscitation and Gastroenterology-led management is required.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Gastroenterology
Recommendations: Admit to an intensive care or step-down unit for close hemodynamic monitoring. Initiate aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation with isotonic crystalloids (e.g., lactated Ringer's, goal 250–300 mL/hr) to correct hypovolemia and prevent organ failure. Maintain NPO status initially; consider nasogastric tube placement for persistent vomiting. Provide adequate analgesia with IV opioids and antiemetics. Do not routinely administer antibiotics unless infection is confirmed; however, if acute cholangitis is suspected (fever, elevated bilirubin), initiate antibiotics and perform urgent ERCP with sphincterotomy. Obtain RUQ ultrasound or MRCP to evaluate for common bile duct stones. Monitor serial BISAP score, organ function (renal, respiratory, cardiovascular), and inflammatory markers. Begin early enteral nutrition once tolerated. After resolution of the acute episode, recommend laparoscopic cholecystectomy during the same admission to prevent recurrent gallstone pancreatitis. Obtain serum triglycerides to rule out hypertriglyceridemia as an alternative etiology. Assess baseline renal function (BUN/creatinine) to guide fluid targets. Check medication list for drug-induced causes (e.g., azathioprine, valproate) and obtain alcohol consumption history. Consider pregnancy status as it would alter imaging and management. Monitor for development of pancreatic necrosis, infected peripancreatic collections, pseudocysts, or abdominal compartment syndrome in the subacute phase; follow-up CT may be needed if clinical deterioration occurs. Consult general surgery early for potential cholecystectomy planning.
Notes: Hypocalcemia may reflect saponification of fat and is a poor prognostic sign. Absence of necrosis on CT does not exclude later development; serial imaging may be warranted. Persistent organ failure >48 hours (e.g., ongoing hypotension requiring vasopressors, respiratory or renal failure) warrants ICU-level care and consideration of surgical intervention for necrotizing or infected collections. The patient's age (42) and lack of comorbidities may improve prognosis, but the severity score still indicates high risk. Prior ERCP or sphincterotomy history would influence need for repeat endoscopic intervention. Vaccination status for hepatitis B is relevant if biliary obstruction leads to cholangitis. Sphincter of Oddi dysfunction or microlithiasis should be considered if imaging fails to show ductal stones.
