criterion:
Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.
Judge only whether the expressed level of diagnostic certainty is appropriately calibrated to the information available.
Mark criteria_met = true if the applicable branch is satisfied and neither failure above is present.
Mark criteria_met = false otherwise.

criterion:
This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.

Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.
Non-stigmatizing description: where the case includes sexual history, substance or alcohol use, tobacco use, body weight, adherence to treatment, or mental health, the protocol describes these as clinical findings. Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.

Naming an action without any such framing does not satisfy this property.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.

A 28-yr-old man comes to the outpatient clinic for evaluation of a lump in his right testis. About 1
month ago, while taking a shower, he noted a hard area in his right testis that felt "like a
marble." He had never noticed this before and decided to wait and see if anything would
change. When the mass did not go away, he scheduled this appointment. Today, he states the
lump is not painful or tender to the touch and has not changed in size. He has had annual
physical exams and was never told that a lump was present. Four years ago, he had a scrotal
ultrasound following a brief episode of scrotal discomfort after competing in a bicycle race; the
result of the ultrasound was normal.

Review of Systems:
General: Overall feels well. Denies any weight loss, fevers, or chills.

Skin: Denies rashes, itching, or other lesions.

HEENT: Noncontributory

Pulmonary: No cough or shortness of breath.

Cardiovascular: No palpitations or chest pain.

Gastrointestinal: Good appetite, bowel movements are normal. Denies nausea or vomiting.
Denies abdominal or flank pain.

Genitourinary: No dysuria, hematuria, frequency, or urgency. No urethral discharge.

Musculoskeletal: No back or joint pain, no leg swelling.

Neurologic: Noncontributory

Psychiatric: Noncontributory

Past Medical History:
Medical history: No reported medical history. Denies history of urinary tract infections, difficulty
with urination, immunosuppressive disorders, or sexually transmitted infections.

Surgical history: Rotator cuff repair 4 yr ago; left inguinal hernia repair as a child.

Medications: Occasional NSAIDs.

Allergies: No known drug allergies.

Family history: Mother and father healthy. No history of genitourinary malignancies in any
known relatives.

Social history: He denies current or previous tobacco use. He exercises almost every day with a
combination of weight training and cardio. He works primarily at a desk job with somewhat
frequent travel. All relevant immunizations are up to date. He denies exposure to any sick
contacts. He has had unprotected sex only with his wife for the past 3 yr.

Physical Examination:
General appearance: Thin male who appears fatigued and older than stated age; in no apparent
respiratory distress.

Vital signs:
Temperature: 37° C
Pulse: 60 beats/min
BP: 112/65 mm Hg
Respirations: 16/min
Height: 6'
Weight: 180 lb
BMI: 24.4

Skin: Warm and dry to the touch.

HEENT: Nasopharynx appears normal; no neck masses or lymphadenopathy.

Pulmonary: Breath sounds present and equal bilaterally. No stridor, rales, or wheezing.

Cardiovascular: Heart rate is regular; radial and dorsalis pedis pulses are present and equal
bilaterally; no pedal edema.

Gastrointestinal: Abdomen is not distended; there are no ecchymoses. Normal bowel sounds

smooth and nontender. Left epididymis is normal in texture and nontender. Right testis has firm
mass in the midsection that is nontender on palpation. Right epididymis is normal in texture and
nontender. There are no palpable inguinal lymph nodes. No urethral discharge.

Musculoskeletal: No costovertebral angle tenderness.

Neurologic: Unremarkable

Mental status: Alert and oriented to person, place, and time.

Cystic testicular mass

Hydrocele

Inguinal hernia

winner_protocol:
Age: 28 years

Sex: Male

Complaint: A hard, painless, non-tender lump in the right testis, present for about 1 month, described as feeling "like a marble," with no change in size and no associated pain.

Analysis: The patient presents with a hard, painless, non-tender intratesticular mass in the right testis that has persisted for about 1 month. This is a classic presentation for testicular cancer (germ cell tumor) in a young man within the peak incidence age range of 15–35 years. The scrotal ultrasonography demonstrates a solid testicular mass, which is highly suspicious for malignancy. The prior normal scrotal ultrasound 4 years ago (performed after a bicycle race) indicates this is a new development, supporting neoplastic growth rather than a congenital anomaly. The absence of inflammatory symptoms, urethral discharge, dysuria, and normal urinary symptoms makes epididymitis or sexually transmitted infection unlikely. Differential considerations include germ cell tumors (seminoma, non-seminomatous), Leydig cell tumor, Sertoli cell tumor, testicular lymphoma, benign intratesticular lesions (e.g., epidermoid cyst), and, less commonly, extratesticular processes such as epididymal mass, hydrocele, or inguinal hernia. No risk factors for testicular cancer (e.g., cryptorchidism, family history) are present, but the absence of risk factors does not exclude malignancy. The lack of back pain, abdominal pain, or lymphadenopathy suggests no obvious metastatic disease at presentation, but staging imaging is still required.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Serum tumor markers (alpha-fetoprotein [AFP], beta-human chorionic gonadotropin [β-hCG], lactate dehydrogenase [LDH]); staging imaging (CT of chest, abdomen, and pelvis; chest X-ray if CT not immediately available); baseline labs (CBC, CMP); pre-operative semen analysis for possible sperm banking.

Conclusion: The patient has a solid intratesticular mass highly suggestive of testicular cancer (germ cell tumor). This requires prompt, non-emergent urological evaluation and management with radical inguinal orchiectomy, which is both diagnostic and therapeutic.

Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care

Subclinical specialization: Urology

Recommendations: Arrange prompt (within days) referral to urology for radical inguinal orchiectomy. Order serum tumor markers (AFP, β-hCG, LDH) and staging CT of chest/abdomen/pelvis prior to surgery. Discuss fertility preservation (sperm banking) and offer it before surgery. Avoid transscrotal biopsy or scrotal exploration due to the risk of tumor seeding and altered lymphatic drainage, which can compromise staging and increase recurrence risk. Provide psychosocial support and counseling regarding sexual function and body image after orchiectomy. Assess for risk factors such as cryptorchidism (including corrected) and infertility history, which are important but were not assessed. Consider baseline testosterone level assessment given the potential impact of orchiectomy on hormonal status. Document testicular size and consistency of the contralateral testis for baseline. Follow-up includes surveillance with serial tumor markers, physical exams, and imaging (chest X-ray, CT scans) based on stage and risk of relapse per guidelines.

Notes: The patient appears fatigued and older than stated age, which may be a subtle sign of systemic disease or malignancy. The absence of back pain, abdominal pain, or lymphadenopathy suggests no obvious metastatic disease at presentation, but staging imaging is still required. Delays beyond a week are inappropriate. Consider genetic counseling if familial testicular cancer is suspected despite negative family history. Consideration of HIV or other immunosuppressive states, which can alter tumor biology, though not reported.

Age: 7 years

Sex: Female

Complaint: Abrupt onset of fever (oral temperature 101°F / 38.5°C), nausea, vomiting, and sore throat, with exudative pharyngitis and enlarged cervical lymph nodes; the child denies cough, rhinorrhea, or nasal congestion.

Analysis: The clinical presentation is classic for acute group A streptococcal (GAS) pharyngitis: abrupt fever, sore throat with exudative pharyngitis, and tender cervical lymphadenopathy, in the absence of viral upper respiratory symptoms such as cough or rhinorrhea. The positive rapid antigen test for GAS confirms the diagnosis with high specificity, making further diagnostic testing unnecessary. The condition is not immediately life-threatening—there is no airway compromise, drooling, stridor, toxic appearance, or severe dehydration—but it requires timely antibiotic therapy to prevent suppurative and non-suppurative complications, most notably acute rheumatic fever. Differential considerations include viral pharyngitis (e.g., adenovirus, Epstein-Barr virus), infectious mononucleosis, and rarely diphtheria, but the positive rapid antigen test establishes GAS as the causative organism. Red flags that would indicate a more urgent condition include respiratory distress, drooling, muffled voice, stridor, inability to swallow, trismus, uvular deviation, severe neck swelling, or signs of systemic toxicity, which would suggest peritonsillar abscess, retropharyngeal abscess, or airway compromise.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None. The positive rapid antigen test is sufficient for diagnosis; no additional testing is indicated unless complications are suspected or the clinical picture changes.

Conclusion: The patient has acute group A streptococcal pharyngitis, confirmed by a positive rapid antigen test. The condition is non-emergent but requires prompt outpatient management with a 10-day course of antibiotics and supportive care to prevent complications such as acute rheumatic fever, post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, and peritonsillar abscess.

Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care

Subclinical specialization: Pediatrics

Recommendations:
- Prescribe a 10-day course of first-line antibiotic therapy: penicillin V or amoxicillin. Assess for penicillin allergy before prescribing; if allergic, use a macrolide (e.g., azithromycin).
- Provide supportive care: acetaminophen or ibuprofen for pain and fever, and ensure adequate hydration, particularly given the risk of dehydration from vomiting.
- Educate the family on the importance of completing the full antibiotic course to prevent rheumatic fever and other complications.
- Advise isolation precautions: the child should stay home from school for at least 24 hours after starting antibiotics to reduce transmission.
- Instruct the family to return for care if symptoms worsen, new neck swelling develops, or fever persists beyond 48–72 hours.
- Assess for red flags of deep neck space infection (severe pain, drooling, voice changes, trismus, uvular deviation) and for signs of scarlet fever (rash), which would not change treatment.
- Inquire about symptomatic household contacts with GAS infection and consider testing/treatment if indicated.
- Ensure the child's vaccination status is up to date (e.g., diphtheria).
- Monitor for complications of untreated or inadequately treated GAS: acute rheumatic fever, post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, and peritonsillar abscess.
- No routine test of cure is needed; follow-up is only required if symptoms fail to improve or red flags develop.

Notes:
- Consider PANDAS only if sudden-onset neuropsychiatric symptoms develop, which is not relevant to this case.
- Family history of rheumatic fever or recent streptococcal infections may influence the urgency of treatment.
- None other.

Age: 70
Sex: Male
Complaint: Acute-onset nausea, vomiting, right-sided weakness, and difficulty speaking and comprehending language (aphasia), progressing from mild slurred speech to severe aphasia and right arm paralysis over several minutes, in a patient with chronic hypertension, atrial fibrillation, and warfarin use.
Analysis: The sudden onset and rapid progression of focal neurological deficits (right-sided weakness and aphasia) in a patient with atrial fibrillation strongly suggest an acute ischemic stroke, most likely cardioembolic, involving the left middle cerebral artery territory. The progression over minutes is typical of acute cerebral ischemia. The most critical differential is intracranial hemorrhage, which must be excluded given the patient's anticoagulation with warfarin and vomiting. Other stroke mimics to consider include hypoglycemia, seizure with Todd's paralysis, complex migraine, brain tumor, and metabolic encephalopathy, though these are less likely given the progressive focal deficits. The warfarin use is a key consideration: it raises the likelihood of hemorrhagic stroke and complicates thrombolytic decision-making, as an elevated INR (>1.7) contraindicates IV thrombolysis.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Non-contrast CT head (to rule out hemorrhage), CT angiography (if large vessel occlusion is suspected), point-of-care blood glucose, INR/PT, complete blood count, basic metabolic panel, and renal function tests.
Conclusion: Acute left hemispheric ischemic stroke, likely cardioembolic, involving the left middle cerebral artery territory, in a patient on warfarin. This is a time-critical emergency requiring immediate evaluation for reperfusion therapy, with hemorrhage and stroke mimics as key differentials.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Neurology
Recommendations: Activate the stroke code and stroke team immediately. Maintain airway, breathing, and circulation, with attention to airway protection given vomiting. Check blood glucose to exclude hypoglycemia. Obtain non-contrast CT head emergently to differentiate ischemic from hemorrhagic stroke; if large vessel occlusion is suspected, proceed with CT angiography. Check INR urgently given warfarin use; IV thrombolysis is indicated only if within the therapeutic window and INR ≤1.7. Consider mechanical thrombectomy if a large vessel occlusion is present. Manage blood pressure per stroke guidelines (e.g., keep systolic BP <185 mmHg if thrombolysis is planned). If hemorrhage is confirmed, initiate reversal of anticoagulation (e.g., vitamin K, prothrombin complex concentrate). For secondary prevention, re-evaluate anticoagulation strategy for atrial fibrillation (warfarin vs DOAC), ensure strict blood pressure control, and initiate statin therapy.
Notes: Warfarin use increases bleeding risk and complicates treatment: if hemorrhagic stroke is confirmed, reversal agents may be needed; if ischemic stroke is confirmed, IV thrombolysis is generally contraindicated if INR >1.7, altering treatment options. Time-sensitive interventions require parallel processing of imaging and coagulation status.

Sex: Female
Complaint: Itchy red rash on both wrists for 4 days, appearing after daily wear of a newly purchased costume jewelry bracelet, with well-demarcated erythematous patches and mild scaling at the contact sites.
Analysis: The clinical picture is classic for allergic contact dermatitis, most likely due to nickel in the costume jewelry bracelet. The strongest supporting facts are the clear temporal relationship between wearing the new bracelet and the onset of the rash, the pruritic, well-demarcated erythematous patches localized precisely to the areas of bracelet contact on both wrists, and the absence of vesiculation, weeping, excoriation, or secondary infection. The mild scaling without vesiculation suggests a subacute or mild allergic reaction rather than a severe acute one. The patient has no history of eczema, which makes atopic dermatitis less likely, though it remains a consideration. Main differential considerations include irritant contact dermatitis (less likely given the delayed onset, pruritus, and lack of exposure to harsh chemicals), atopic dermatitis, psoriasis, and tinea corporis; less likely possibilities include drug eruption and early cellulitis, though the localized distribution and absence of systemic signs argue against these. No red flags are present: there is no fever, rapid spread, intense pain, vesiculation, purulence, or systemic symptoms, and the rash does not represent an acute systemic allergic reaction (no angioedema, respiratory distress, or hypotension). The condition is non-urgent and self-care appropriate.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None. The diagnosis is clinical; no diagnostic tests are indicated at this stage. Patch testing may be considered later if the rash persists, recurs despite avoidance, or if the diagnosis remains uncertain.
Conclusion: This is a localized, mild-to-subacute allergic contact dermatitis, most likely due to nickel in the costume jewelry bracelet. The condition is non-urgent, self-care appropriate, and does not require immediate medical intervention. Definitive management and any future patch testing fall within the scope of dermatology, though primary care can initiate care.
Emergency type: Self-care appropriate
Subclinical specialization: Dermatology
Recommendations: Instruct the patient to remove and discontinue wearing the offending bracelet immediately. Advise avoidance of nickel-containing jewelry and use of hypoallergenic alternatives; recommend checking jewelry labels for nickel content. Sex: Female
Complaint: A cluster of small fluid-filled vesicles on an erythematous base at the vermilion border of the left lower lip, preceded by a tingling and burning sensation that began the day prior. The patient reports similar episodes approximately twice a year for the past 5 years and notes increased work-related stress. No fever, sore throat, oral ulcers, facial nerve involvement, lymphadenopathy, or intraoral lesions are present.

Analysis: The clinical presentation is classic for recurrent herpes labialis (cold sore) caused by HSV-1. The strongest supporting facts are the characteristic prodrome of tingling and burning at the site, the clustered vesicles on an erythematous base located at the vermilion border, the recurrent pattern (twice yearly for 5 years), and the absence of systemic symptoms or red-flag findings. The reported increase in work stress is a well-documented precipitant of HSV-1 reactivation. The diagnosis is clinical and does not require laboratory confirmation in this typical presentation. Main differential considerations include herpes zoster (dermatomal distribution, deeper pain, unlikely given recurrent history and location), impetigo (honey-colored crusting), contact dermatitis (pruritic, exposure history), allergic cheilitis, aphthous ulcer (painful oral ulcer, not vesicular, not on vermilion border), herpangina (posterior oropharyngeal vesicles with systemic symptoms), and early Stevens-Johnson syndrome (mucosal involvement, systemic symptoms). These are distinguished by morphology, distribution, systemic features, and history; the current case strongly favors HSV-1.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None. Diagnosis is clinical. PCR or viral culture of vesicular fluid is reserved for atypical presentations, immunocompromised patients, or diagnostic uncertainty, none of which apply here.

Conclusion: This is a typical episode of recurrent herpes labialis (HSV-1) in an otherwise healthy 28-year-old woman. The condition is localized, self-limited, and non-urgent. It can be managed with early antiviral therapy and supportive care, with patient education on trigger avoidance and contagion. No emergency intervention or routine diagnostic testing is indicated.

Emergency type: Self-care appropriate
Subclinical specialization: Dermatology

Recommendations:
1. Initiate early antiviral therapy at the prodrome stage to reduce duration and severity. Oral antiviral therapy (e.g., valacyclovir 2 g single dose or 1 g twice daily for 1–3 days, or acyclovir) is first-line for systemic effect; topical antivirals (e.g., penciclovir or acyclovir cream) are acceptable for mild cases. The choice may be guided by episode severity and patient preference.
2. Provide supportive care: analgesics for pain, lip moisturizers, and avoidance of triggers (stress, UV/sun exposure, illness, local trauma).
3. Educate the patient on the contagious nature of HSV-1: avoid kissing, sharing utensils, or touching lesions; practice strict hand hygiene to prevent autoinoculation to the eyes or other sites.
4. Counsel on trigger management, including stress reduction techniques and sun protection (e.g., lip balm with SPF), to reduce recurrence frequency.
5. Advise the patient to seek medical evaluation if any red-flag signs develop: ocular involvement (eye pain, photophobia, redness), fever or systemic illness, rapid lesion spread, extensive mucosal ulceration, facial nerve palsy, or no improvement after 48 hours.
6. Assess immunocompromised status (e.g., HIV, chemotherapy) and pregnancy status, as these may require systemic antiviral therapy, closer monitoring, or special consideration (neonatal herpes risk if active lesions near delivery).
7. Consider suppressive antiviral therapy if recurrences become frequent (≥6 per year) or if quality of life is significantly impacted.

winner_protocol:
Age: 50 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: Worsening lower back pain radiating bilaterally to both legs over 3 days, progressive bilateral leg weakness, and difficulty urinating since yesterday, in a man with a history of lumbar disc disease and two prior episodes of sciatica managed conservatively.
Analysis: The clinical presentation is classic for cauda equina syndrome. Key red flags include bilateral lower extremity weakness (3/5 in ankle dorsiflexion and plantarflexion), saddle anesthesia (decreased perianal sensation), reduced anal sphincter tone on rectal exam, and urinary retention confirmed by a post-void residual of 650 mL. Diminished patellar and absent Achilles reflexes bilaterally indicate lower motor neuron involvement at L4 and S1 levels, respectively. The wide-based unsteady gait reflects weakness and possible proprioceptive loss. MRI of the lumbar spine confirms the diagnosis by demonstrating a large L4-L5 central disc herniation with severe compression of the cauda equina nerve roots. This is a surgical emergency; the acute onset of urinary retention and progressive motor deficits mandate urgent decompression, ideally within 24 hours of symptom onset, to maximize recovery of bladder, bowel, and motor function. Differential diagnoses include spinal epidural abscess, spinal tumor, transverse myelitis, severe lumbar spinal stenosis, and conus medullaris syndrome; however, the MRI findings of a central disc herniation with cauda equina compression are diagnostic, and the absence of fever makes infection less likely though not impossible.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: MRI of the lumbar spine (already performed and sufficient for diagnosis); CBC, basic metabolic panel, coagulation profile (PT/INR, aPTT, platelet count), ESR/CRP, blood cultures (if infection suspected), type and screen; urinalysis and culture; post-void residual bladder scan (already performed); ECG and chest X-ray if indicated for pre-operative optimization.
Conclusion: This patient has cauda equina syndrome secondary to a large L4-L5 central disc herniation with severe compression of the cauda equina nerve roots, confirmed by MRI. The presence of bilateral leg weakness, saddle anesthesia, reduced anal sphincter tone, and urinary retention with a post-void residual of 650 mL constitutes a surgical emergency. Urgent surgical decompression, ideally within 24 hours of symptom onset, is required to prevent permanent neurological deficits, particularly of bladder and bowel function. The patient must be hospitalized immediately for continuous monitoring, pre-operative optimization, and timely surgical intervention.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Orthopedics
Recommendations:
1. Hospitalize the patient immediately for continuous neurological monitoring (motor strength, reflexes, sensation) at least every 2 hours.
2. Insert an indwelling Foley catheter to decompress the bladder and monitor urine output; manage urinary retention proactively.
3. Keep the patient NPO in preparation for urgent surgery.
4. Consult neurosurgery or orthopedic spine surgery immediately for urgent surgical decompression (laminectomy with discectomy at L4-L5), ideally within 24 hours of symptom onset and no later than 48 hours.
5. Obtain baseline labs (CBC, metabolic panel, coagulation profile, ESR/CRP, blood cultures if infection suspected, type and screen) and urinalysis/culture.
6. Provide adequate analgesia (IV opioids or NSAIDs) while avoiding excessive sedation that could mask neurological deterioration.
7. Do NOT administer systemic corticosteroids without surgical consultation, as evidence for benefit is lacking and potential harm exists.
8. Initiate mechanical DVT prophylaxis (sequential compression devices); add pharmacologic prophylaxis (low-dose LMWH) post-operatively once hemostasis is secured.
9. Assess bowel function: document stool pattern, perform digital rectal exam, and start stool softeners or laxatives to prevent constipation and fecal impaction.
10. Review all current medications, especially anticoagulants and antiplatelet agents; hold or bridge anticoagulation per surgical protocol.
11. Perform pre-operative optimization: correct anemia and electrolyte abnormalities, ensure adequate hydration, and assess cardiac/pulmonary risk (ECG, chest X-ray if indicated).
12. Obtain informed consent, discussing risks (neurologic worsening, paralysis, incontinence, infection, CSF leak, need for re-operation), benefits, and alternatives, emphasizing that delayed decompression increases the risk of permanent deficits.
13. Plan post-operative rehabilitation: early mobilization with physical therapy, gait training, bladder retraining (intermittent catheterization if needed), bowel retraining, and occupational therapy for activities of daily living.
14. Monitor for post-operative complications: wound infection, CSF leak, and neurological decline; obtain follow-up imaging (MRI or CT) if post-operative neurological deterioration occurs.
15. Address comorbidities (e.g., diabetes, immunosuppression) that may affect surgical timing, infection risk, and neurological recovery.
Notes: The duration of symptoms (>48 hours from onset of urinary retention) worsens the prognosis for neurological recovery, heightening the urgency of decompression. The absence of trauma history does not exclude severe disc herniation, as it can occur spontaneously in predisposed individuals. Bilateral involvement and saddle anesthesia distinguish this from typical radiculopathy and confirm central compression. Diminished patellar reflexes suggest L4 involvement; absent Achilles reflexes suggest S1 involvement. The wide-based unsteady gait may indicate proprioceptive loss or weakness, warranting assessment for concurrent spinal cord involvement. Lumbar puncture is not indicated given the clear structural lesion on MRI and the risk of herniation with obstructive pathology.

Age: 25

Sex: Female

Complaint: Bilateral thigh soreness beginning approximately 36 hours after a first gym session involving squats and lunges; soreness is worse with movement, particularly going downstairs. No acute injury, popping sensation, bruising, or swelling reported.

Analysis: The presentation is classic for delayed onset muscle soreness (DOMS) from unaccustomed eccentric exercise. Key supporting facts include the 36-hour post-exercise onset, bilateral symmetric involvement of the quadriceps and hamstrings, absence of acute trauma or popping sensation, no swelling, ecchymosis, warmth, or joint effusion, full range of motion with only mild end-range discomfort, and a normal gait. The bilateral symmetric pattern and preserved function make a focal structural injury such as an acute muscle strain or tear unlikely. The main differential considerations include DOMS, acute muscle strain/tear, tendinopathy, stress fracture, inflammatory arthritis, infectious myositis, early rhabdomyolysis, and electrolyte disturbances. The absence of red flags — dark urine, severe or rapidly worsening pain, significant swelling, focal weakness, fever, inability to bear weight, or neurovascular deficits — is reassuring and effectively excludes serious conditions such as rhabdomyolysis or compartment syndrome at this time. No personal or family history of myopathy further reduces, though does not eliminate, the risk of atypical exercise-induced muscle injury.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None. No routine imaging or laboratory tests are indicated for this classic DOMS presentation. If red flags emerge (e.g., dark urine, weakness, significant swelling), serum creatine kinase and urinalysis for myoglobin should be considered.

Conclusion: This is a benign, self-limited case of delayed onset muscle soreness (DOMS) resulting from unaccustomed eccentric exercise (squats and lunges). The clinical picture is consistent with DOMS, and no urgent or emergent intervention is needed. Management is appropriate for self-care with patient education and symptom monitoring.

Emergency type: Self-care appropriate

Subclinical specialization: General Medicine

Recommendations: Reassure the patient that DOMS is a normal, self-limited response to unaccustomed eccentric exercise. Advise relative rest and avoidance of intense activity until symptoms resolve, along with gentle stretching and adequate hydration. Over-the-counter analgesics (acetaminophen or NSAIDs) may be used as needed for symptom relief; caution the patient about NSAID use, particularly regarding gastrointestinal or renal side effects if dehydrated. Plan a gradual return to exercise with progressive overload and proper warm-up to prevent recurrence. Explicitly counsel the patient to monitor for red flags — dark (tea-colored) urine, severe or worsening pain, significant swelling, muscle weakness, fever, or inability to bear weight — and to seek re-evaluation promptly if any develop, as these could indicate evolving rhabdomyolysis or another serious condition. Also ask about recent medication or supplement use to further exclude myotoxic triggers. Emphasize that hydration status and electrolyte balance influence muscle recovery and rhabdomyolysis risk. Note that baseline fitness level and prior conditioning affect susceptibility to DOMS, and that eccentric exercises like squats and lunges are particularly associated with this condition. Age: 26
Sex: Female
Complaint: A 26-year-old female marathon runner presents with a 3-week history of gradually worsening pain over the dorsum of the right foot, localized to the region of the third metatarsal. The pain initially occurred only during long runs but is now present with walking and at rest. She significantly increased her training mileage six weeks ago in preparation for an upcoming marathon. She has a history of irregular menstrual periods and follows a restrictive diet. Examination reveals focal tenderness and mild soft-tissue swelling over the mid-shaft of the third metatarsal, with pain elicited by the tuning fork test and axial loading of the third toe. BMI is 19. Foot radiographs obtained one week ago at another facility were normal.
Analysis: The clinical presentation is most consistent with a stress fracture of the third metatarsal (march fracture). The strongest supporting facts include the recent significant increase in training mileage, the gradual onset of focal bony tenderness over the mid-shaft of the third metatarsal, and positive provocative tests (tuning fork test and axial loading of the third toe). Normal initial radiographs do not exclude a stress fracture, as imaging findings often lag behind clinical symptoms by several weeks. The patient's low BMI (19), history of irregular menstrual periods, and restrictive diet raise significant concern for the female athlete triad (low energy availability, menstrual dysfunction, and low bone mineral density), which is a major risk factor for stress fractures. Main differential considerations include metatarsalgia, Morton's neuroma, extensor tendinopathy, sesamoiditis, early osteomyelitis, and bone tumor (e.g., osteoid osteoma); however, the specific location, mechanism of injury, and positive bone-pain tests favor a stress fracture. No immediate red flags such as signs of infection, neurovascular compromise, or severe deformity are present, but the female athlete triad represents a significant underlying risk factor that must be addressed.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: MRI of the foot (preferred) to confirm the stress fracture and assess the extent of bone marrow edema and cortical changes; bone scintigraphy as an alternative if MRI is unavailable; CT may be considered if delineation of a fracture line is needed; basic labs (CBC, ESR/CRP) only if infection is suspected; DEXA scan for bone mineral density assessment given the concern for the female athlete triad; nutritional assessment for calcium, vitamin D, and overall caloric intake.
Conclusion: The patient most likely has a stress fracture of the third metatarsal (march fracture), a non-emergent but time-sensitive musculoskeletal injury. Prompt orthopedic evaluation and management are required to prevent progression to a complete fracture, nonunion, or delayed healing. The underlying female athlete triad (low energy availability, menstrual dysfunction, and low bone mineral density) is a critical contributing factor that must be addressed to prevent recurrence and long-term morbidity.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Orthopedics
Recommendations: 1) Activity modification: temporarily cease running and reduce weight-bearing activities to allow bone healing. 2) Protected weight-bearing with a stiff-soled shoe or walking boot; consider non-weight-bearing if pain is severe. 3) Pain control with NSAIDs as needed and ice for symptom relief. 4) Referral for advanced imaging (MRI preferred) to confirm the diagnosis and guide definitive management. 5) Orthopedic evaluation for immobilization decisions, weight-bearing status, and a structured return-to-sport protocol. 6) Address the female athlete triad: evaluate menstrual irregularity, assess energy availability and nutritional status, consider calcium and vitamin D supplementation, consider DEXA scan for bone mineral density, provide dietary counseling, and consider endocrinology input if menstrual irregularities persist. 7) Screen for endocrine disorders (e.g., hypothyroidism) if menstrual irregularities persist. 8) Develop a progressive training plan with appropriate footwear, and consider running surface and gait mechanics as contributing factors. 9) Educate the patient on gradual return to training to prevent recurrence.
Notes: Normal radiographs do not exclude a stress fracture; advanced imaging is needed if clinical suspicion remains high. The tuning fork test and axial loading are supportive clinical tests but are not definitive. The female athlete triad is underdiagnosed; failure to address it may lead to recurrent injuries and long-term morbidity. Delayed diagnosis can lead to nonunion, chronic pain, or need for surgical intervention. One expert considered the female athlete triad a red flag, whereas others viewed it as a risk factor but not an immediate red flag; this divergence does not alter the management plan. One expert also included referred pain from lumbar spine or nerve entrapment in the differential, which was not mentioned by others and is less likely given the focal findings.

Age: 6 months

Sex: Male

Complaint: Small red bumps on the neck and chest noticed today in a 6-month-old male infant, occurring in the setting of a hot climate, broken air conditioning for 3 days, and overdressing with multiple layers.

Analysis: The clinical presentation of numerous small erythematous papules and tiny vesicles clustered on the neck, upper chest, and skin folds, in an afebrile (37.1°C), alert, active, and well-hydrated infant with normal feeding and wet diapers, is classic for miliaria rubra (heat rash). The key supporting facts are the hot environment, the broken air conditioning, the multiple layers of clothing, and the distribution in skin folds — all consistent with sweat duct occlusion and inflammation. The infant's age (6 months) makes heat rash common due to immature sweat ducts. The absence of fever and systemic symptoms argues against an infectious process. Main differential considerations include viral exanthem, bacterial folliculitis, allergic contact dermatitis, scabies, atopic dermatitis, neonatal acne, and transient neonatal pustular melanosis; however, the history of heat exposure and the clinical pattern strongly favor miliaria rubra. Although rare, disseminated viral infections (e.g., enterovirus) can present with vesicular rashes and must be considered if fever or systemic symptoms develop.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None. The diagnosis is clinical; no routine diagnostic tests are indicated. Conditional testing (e.g., skin scraping or culture) is only warranted if atypical features develop or secondary infection is suspected.

Conclusion: This is a benign, self-limited case of miliaria rubra (heat rash) in a well-appearing 6-month-old infant, triggered by excessive heat and overdressing. Management is primarily environmental and supportive, with no urgent medical intervention required. The condition is expected to resolve with cooling measures and removal of excess clothing. The main risk is secondary bacterial infection (e.g., impetigo) if lesions become pustular, eroded, or crusted, particularly in warm, moist environments.

Emergency type: Self-care appropriate

Subclinical specialization: Pediatrics

Recommendations:
- Advise the mother to cool the environment (repair or supplement the air conditioning, use fans) and remove excess layers of clothing.
- Dress the infant in lightweight, loose, breathable fabrics; avoid tight or occlusive clothing.
- Keep the skin dry and allow affected areas to air out.
- Cool compresses or lukewarm baths may provide symptomatic relief.
- A thin layer of a mild barrier ointment (e.g., zinc oxide) may be applied if irritation is present; avoid heavy creams or ointments, which can occlude sweat ducts and worsen miliaria.
- No antihistamines or topical antibiotics are needed unless there is evidence of secondary infection.
- Reassure the mother that the rash is benign and self-limited; educate on prevention (avoiding overdressing in hot climates) and on red-flag signs.
- Monitor for signs of secondary bacterial infection (pustules, crusting, spreading erythema) or systemic symptoms (fever, lethargy, poor feeding, increased irritability); if these develop, seek prompt medical evaluation.
- Schedule routine follow-up in 2–3 days if the rash is not improving; if the rash persists beyond a few days despite cooling measures, reconsider the diagnosis.
- Address additional considerations: confirm immunization status is up to date; inquire about prior history of atopic dermatitis or other skin conditions in the child or family; ask about recent use of new soaps, detergents, lotions, or fabrics that could cause contact dermatitis; assess for sweating or diaphoresis in affected areas; ask about exposure to other children or caregivers with contagious skin conditions; and confirm baseline hydration status beyond normal wet diapers (e.g., urine output, skin turgor).

Notes: The absence of pruritus or irritability is reassuring but not definitive, as infants may not scratch visibly. Miliaria can progress to deeper forms (e.g., miliaria profunda) if heat exposure continues. Tiny vesicles may rupture, leaving superficial erosions that can become infected; monitor for secondary bacterial infection. If fever or systemic symptoms develop, consider disseminated viral infections (e.g., enterovirus) in the differential.

Step 2: Is that level of care correct for this case, and do the Recommendations act on it? Exactly one of the three situations below applies to any given case, and the protocol is judged against that one:

Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.
- Requires non-emergent care: The condition does not require emergency intervention, but cannot be adequately managed by the patient at home with only limited outpatient supervision. It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.
- Self-care appropriate: The condition can be safely managed outside an inpatient or day-hospital setting. Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. The Recommendations must not direct the patient to inpatient or emergency care unless escalation is conditional on a specified new or worsening clinical feature.
If not, fail.

criterion:
Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.
Judge only whether the expressed level of diagnostic certainty is appropriately calibrated to the information available.

Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.
Non-stigmatizing description: where the case includes sexual history, substance or alcohol use, tobacco use, body weight, adherence to treatment, or mental health, the protocol describes these as clinical findings. Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.
Expectation-setting: the protocol tells the reader what to expect, by stating at least one of the following: the expected course or duration of the condition, the signs that should prompt the patient to seek care again or sooner, or what the proposed next step will involve for the patient. Naming an action without any such framing does not satisfy this property.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.

Age: 24
Sex: Male
Complaint: Sudden onset of shortness of breath and sharp, constant, mild, nonradiating pain in the spine and right side of the back, present at rest and worse with exertion; symptoms began during a 2-mile run the previous day and persisted overnight, with worsening dyspnea prompting the ED visit.
Analysis: The clinical picture is most consistent with a primary spontaneous pneumothorax on the right side. Supporting facts include the patient's young age, male sex, smoking history (7–10 cigarettes/day), acute exertional onset of dyspnea with ipsilateral back pain, unilateral decreased breath sounds on the right, and mild hypoxia (SpO2 94% on room air) in an otherwise well-appearing patient without fever, cough, or wheezing. The absence of trauma, normal vital signs, lack of tracheal deviation, and symmetric pulses argue against traumatic pneumothorax, tension physiology at presentation, massive pulmonary embolism, or cardiac tamponade. The sharp, nonradiating back pain not worsened by movement is consistent with pleuritic pain from a pneumothorax rather than musculoskeletal pain. Differential considerations include pulmonary embolism, pleuritis, pneumonia, pleural effusion, aortic dissection, pericarditis, COVID-19, asthma/COPD exacerbation, and musculoskeletal back pain; however, the absence of fever, cough, chest pain, and cardiovascular abnormalities, combined with unilateral decreased breath sounds, makes pneumothorax the leading diagnosis. Red-flag complications to monitor include tension pneumothorax, rapid enlargement of the pneumothorax, progressive respiratory failure, hemothorax, and pneumomediastinum.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Bedside postero-anterior chest X-ray (first-line imaging to confirm pneumothorax and assess size); bedside thoracic ultrasound as a rapid alternative, especially if the patient becomes unstable; continuous pulse oximetry and vital-sign monitoring; IV access supplies; supplemental oxygen; analgesia; equipment for needle thoracostomy and chest tube insertion prepared in advance.
Conclusion: The patient most likely has a primary spontaneous pneumothorax on the right side, given the classic presentation of acute exertional dyspnea, ipsilateral back pain, unilateral decreased breath sounds, and mild hypoxia in a young male smoker. The condition is emergent, requiring immediate ED evaluation and monitoring due to the risk of progression to tension physiology or respiratory failure. Chest X-ray is the initial diagnostic test to confirm the diagnosis and guide disposition.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Emergency
Recommendations: 1) Administer supplemental oxygen to treat hypoxemia and promote resorption of pleural air. 2) Provide continuous pulse-oximetry and vital-sign monitoring, and establish IV access. 3) Provide analgesia as needed for comfort and ventilation. 4) Prepare for needle thoracostomy if tension physiology develops, and place a chest tube if the pneumothorax is large or symptomatic. 5) Obtain a chest X-ray promptly to confirm the diagnosis and assess pneumothorax size; use bedside ultrasound if the patient becomes unstable. 6) Determine disposition based on pneumothorax size and clinical stability: small (<2 cm rim width) and stable pneumothorax with minimal symptoms may be managed outpatient with close follow-up (repeat chest X-ray in 24–48 hours, smoking-cessation counseling, and pulmonology referral); moderate-to-large or symptomatic pneumothorax, or any pneumothorax that does not resolve, warrants admission for observation, possible chest-tube placement, and serial imaging. Given this patient's persistent dyspnea and SpO2 of 94%, admission for observation and management is the safer choice. 7) Provide smoking-cessation counseling, as smoking is a significant risk factor for recurrence. 8) Arrange outpatient pulmonology follow-up for all patients. 9) Monitor for red-flag complications including tension pneumothorax, massive pulmonary embolism, progressive respiratory failure, hemothorax, and rapid enlargement of the pneumothorax; consider advanced imaging (e.g., CT) for pulmonary embolism only if clinical suspicion remains after initial imaging is inconclusive.
Notes: The patient's height and body habitus are not specified; a tall, thin build would increase risk for spontaneous pneumothorax. Percussion findings (e.g., hyperresonance) were not documented and would support the diagnosis. Recent runny nose may suggest viral pleuritis as an alternative cause, but is likely incidental. Family history of lung cancer is noted but not directly relevant to the acute presentation. Back pain as a presenting feature of pneumothorax is underrecognized and may mimic musculoskeletal or spinal pathology.

winner_protocol:
Age: 45 years

Sex: Male

Complaint: A farmer collapsed in the field approximately 30 minutes after spraying crops with an organophosphate insecticide without adequate protective equipment. He initially complained of blurred vision and headache, then developed profuse sweating, drooling, vomiting, and became unresponsive. On arrival he is obtunded with labored breathing, bradycardia, hypotension, hypoxia, copious secretions, miosis, and fasciculations.

Analysis: The clinical picture is a classic cholinergic toxidrome from acute organophosphate poisoning. Strong supporting facts include the recent exposure to an organophosphate insecticide without protection, the garlic-like odor on the damp clothing, and the constellation of muscarinic effects (miosis, bradycardia, copious oral and bronchial secretions, wheezing, vomiting, incontinence, hypotension), nicotinic effects (fasciculations of extremities and face), and central nervous system effects (obtundation, unresponsiveness). The severe respiratory compromise (shallow breathing at RR 12, SpO2 84%, audible secretions, diffuse wheezing and crackles) indicates impending respiratory failure. Main differential considerations include other cholinesterase inhibitors such as carbamate poisoning and nerve agents, which can mimic this toxidrome; also considered are opioid overdose, myasthenia gravis crisis, intracranial catastrophe (e.g., brainstem stroke), severe anaphylaxis, acute myocardial infarction, sepsis, hypoglycemia, and acute stroke. However, the exposure history and classic cholinergic findings make acute organophosphate poisoning the most likely diagnosis. Treatment must not be delayed for confirmatory testing.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Pulse oximetry and continuous cardiac monitoring; arterial blood gas; ECG; chest X-ray; serum (red blood cell or plasma) cholinesterase levels (confirmatory, but must not delay treatment); basic metabolic panel, serum glucose, lactate, and electrolytes (potassium, magnesium); renal function tests; consider toxicology screen if co-exposure is suspected.

Conclusion: This is a life-threatening emergency of acute organophosphate poisoning with a severe cholinergic crisis. The patient is obtunded, hypoxic, hypotensive, bradycardic, and in respiratory failure with excessive secretions, reflecting profound muscarinic, nicotinic, and central effects. Immediate management requires aggressive airway control (already intubated), decontamination, and administration of atropine titrated to drying of secretions and pralidoxime to reactivate cholinesterase, with intensive care unit admission for ongoing monitoring and management of complications such as intermediate syndrome, aspiration pneumonia, arrhythmias, and delayed neuropathy.

Emergency type: Requires emergent care

Subclinical specialization: Emergency

Recommendations: Continue aggressive atropine administration in escalating doses (e.g., 2–5 mg IV every 5 minutes) titrated to drying of secretions, resolution of bradycardia, and improvement in lung sounds; tachycardia is not a contraindication. Continue pralidoxime infusion (e.g., 1–2 g bolus then 0.5–1 g/h) given early before enzyme aging (typically within 24–48 hours) to be effective. Maintain mechanical ventilation with 100% O2 and monitor for prolonged ventilation needs due to respiratory muscle weakness. Administer benzodiazepines for seizures or severe agitation; consider prophylaxis in severe cases. Provide aggressive IV fluids and vasopressors if hypotension persists. Admit to the intensive care unit with continuous ECG and pulse-oximetry monitoring; obtain serial arterial blood gases and repeat serum cholinesterase every 12–24 hours. Monitor for intermediate syndrome (muscle weakness 24–96 hours after exposure) and delayed organophosphate-induced polyneuropathy (1–3 weeks later). Monitor electrolytes (potassium, magnesium) and correct abnormalities to prevent arrhythmias; monitor renal function for possible rhabdomyolysis from fasciculations. Watch for aspiration pneumonia given vomiting and secretions; consider antibiotics if signs of infection develop. Healthcare workers should use protective equipment to avoid secondary contamination until decontamination is complete. Consider activated charcoal if ingestion occurred within the past hour and the airway is protected. Assess the pesticide formulation (e.g., presence of carbamate) to adjust antidote dosing. Consider co-ingestion or mixed exposures (e.g., solvents, other drugs) that may affect management. Arrange follow-up with occupational health and toxicology.

Notes: The garlic-like odor is characteristic but not always present; it supports the diagnosis. Cholinesterase levels are confirmatory but not rapidly available; treatment must not wait for lab results. Atropine should be titrated to drying of secretions, not to a specific heart rate or pupil size.

criterion:
Step 1: Does the Emergency type field contain exactly one of the three permitted labels, namely Self-care appropriate, Requires non-emergent care, or Requires emergent care, with no addition or substitution? If not, fail.
Step 2: Is that level of care correct for this case, and do the Recommendations act on it? Exactly one of the three situations below applies to any given case, and the protocol is judged against that one:
- Requires emergent care: The condition requires immediate medical assessment and/or initiation of treatment because delaying care could reasonably increase the risk of death, irreversible organ damage, serious complication, or rapid clinical deterioration. Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.
- Requires non-emergent care: The condition does not require emergency intervention, but cannot be adequately managed by the patient at home with only limited outpatient supervision. It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.
- Self-care appropriate: The condition can be safely managed outside an inpatient or day-hospital setting. Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. The Recommendations must not direct the patient to inpatient or emergency care unless escalation is conditional on a specified new or worsening clinical feature.
If not, fail.
Under-triage, meaning failure to escalate a condition that needs it, and over-triage, meaning escalation of a condition that does not, are both failures of this criterion. Escalation that is presented conditionally, that is, tied to a stated sign or circumstance, is not over-triage.

If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

criterion:
Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.
Judge only whether the expressed level of diagnostic certainty is appropriately calibrated to the information available.
Mark criteria_met = true if the applicable branch is satisfied and neither failure above is present.
Mark criteria_met = false otherwise.

The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.
Non-stigmatizing description: where the case includes sexual history, substance or alcohol use, tobacco use, body weight, adherence to treatment, or mental health, the protocol describes these as clinical findings. Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.
Expectation-setting: the protocol tells the reader what to expect, by stating at least one of the following: the expected course or duration of the condition, the signs that should prompt the patient to seek care again or sooner, or what the proposed next step will involve for the patient. Naming an action without any such framing does not satisfy this property.

- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.

winner_protocol:
Age: 70 years

Sex: Male

Complaint: Progressive nocturia (waking to urinate) that has increased from 2 to 6 times per night over several years, accompanied by straining to initiate urination and a weak urinary stream. Daytime urinary frequency is not increased, and the patient denies incontinence, dysuria, hematuria, flank pain, or fever.

Analysis: The patient presents with classic lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS) of both obstructive (straining, weak stream) and storage (nocturia) types, which have progressed gradually over years. The digital rectal exam reveals a smooth, enlarged prostate gland estimated at approximately 70 g with no identifiable central sulcus and no nodules or tenderness, findings most consistent with benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH). Urinalysis is negative for blood, leukocyte esterase, nitrites, protein, and bacteria, effectively ruling out urinary tract infection, hematuria, and glycosuria. The serum PSA level of 3.2 ng/mL is mildly elevated but within the age-adjusted range for a 70-year-old man and, combined with a smooth gland, is more consistent with benign enlargement than malignancy, although the family history of prostate cancer (father) warrants continued monitoring. No red flags are present: there is no acute urinary retention (no palpable bladder or suprapubic tenderness), no hematuria, no dysuria, no fever, no flank pain, and no constitutional symptoms. The main differential considerations include BPH (most likely), prostate cancer (lower suspicion given smooth DRE and normal age-adjusted PSA), overactive bladder (unlikely given obstructive symptoms), urethral stricture (less likely given enlarged prostate), neurogenic bladder (no neurologic findings), and nocturnal polyuria from systemic causes such as diabetes or heart failure (not supported by history or review of systems). The patient's atrial fibrillation (not on anticoagulation) and medications (aspirin, avanafil) are relevant to management decisions but do not alter the non-emergent nature of the presentation.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Post-void residual (PVR) measurement by bladder ultrasound; uroflowmetry; serum creatinine to assess for renal impairment from chronic obstruction; repeat PSA in 6–12 months for continued prostate cancer risk stratification given family history. Renal/bladder ultrasound is reserved for cases of elevated PVR or suspected upper tract involvement.

Conclusion: This 70-year-old man has moderate-to-severe lower urinary tract symptoms consistent with benign prostatic hyperplasia, with a 70-g smooth prostate on DRE, negative urinalysis, and mildly elevated but age-appropriate PSA. The condition is chronic, slowly progressive, and without red flags or complications such as acute retention, infection, hematuria, or renal impairment. Management is appropriately initiated in the outpatient setting with medical therapy and monitoring.

Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care

Subclinical specialization: Urology

Recommendations: Initiate medical therapy with an alpha-blocker (e.g., tamsulosin) for rapid symptom relief. Given the estimated prostate size of ~70 g, consider adding a 5-alpha reductase inhibitor (e.g., finasteride) to reduce prostate volume and slow disease progression, either initially or if monotherapy proves insufficient. Counsel on lifestyle modifications, including limiting evening fluid intake and avoiding caffeine before bedtime, to help reduce nocturia. Measure post-void residual and perform uroflowmetry to objectively grade obstruction severity and bladder emptying. Check serum creatinine to exclude renal impairment. Repeat PSA in 6–12 months and discuss prostate cancer screening with the patient given his father's history of prostate cancer; a smooth DRE and normal age-adjusted PSA do not currently warrant biopsy. Caution is needed when combining an alpha-blocker with avanafil (PDE-5 inhibitor) due to additive hypotensive effects; use a low-dose alpha-blocker with careful blood pressure monitoring and consider timing of doses. The patient's atrial fibrillation and lack of anticoagulation represent a separate management issue that should be addressed with his cardiologist, particularly if surgical intervention is ever contemplated, as aspirin may need to be held perioperatively. Re-evaluate in 3–6 months with a symptom score, repeat PVR, and PSA. Escalate care or refer to urology if symptoms remain bothersome or worsen, if acute urinary retention develops, if hematuria or rising PSA (>4 ng/mL) occurs, or if PVR becomes significant (>200 mL).

Notes: The absence of a central sulcus on DRE is consistent with prostatic enlargement but is not specific for malignancy; combined with a normal age-adjusted PSA, it favors benign disease. Recent travel to the western Caribbean raises theoretical infectious concerns, but the negative urinalysis and absence of symptoms do not support an infectious etiology. Aspirin use could theoretically mask microscopic hematuria, though the urinalysis was negative. The patient's active lifestyle and good functional status support a conservative, outpatient approach with close follow-up.

Step 1: Does the Emergency type field contain exactly one of the three permitted labels, namely Self-care appropriate, Requires non-emergent care, or Requires emergent care, with no addition or substitution? If not, fail.
Step 2: Is that level of care correct for this case, and do the Recommendations act on it? Exactly one of the three situations below applies to any given case, and the protocol is judged against that one:
- Requires emergent care: The condition requires immediate medical assessment and/or initiation of treatment because delaying care could reasonably increase the risk of death, irreversible organ damage, serious complication, or rapid clinical deterioration. Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.
- Requires non-emergent care: The condition does not require emergency intervention, but cannot be adequately managed by the patient at home with only limited outpatient supervision. It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.
- Self-care appropriate: The condition can be safely managed outside an inpatient or day-hospital setting. Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. The Recommendations must not direct the patient to inpatient or emergency care unless escalation is conditional on a specified new or worsening clinical feature.
If not, fail.
Under-triage, meaning failure to escalate a condition that needs it, and over-triage, meaning escalation of a condition that does not, are both failures of this criterion. Escalation that is presented conditionally, that is, tied to a stated sign or circumstance, is not over-triage.

criterion:
Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.
Judge only whether the expressed level of diagnostic certainty is appropriately calibrated to the information available.
Mark criteria_met = true if the applicable branch is satisfied and neither failure above is present.
Mark criteria_met = false otherwise.

tags: ['axis:communication_quality']
criterion:
This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.
The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.
Non-stigmatizing description: where the case includes sexual history, substance or alcohol use, tobacco use, body weight, adherence to treatment, or mental health, the protocol describes these as clinical findings. Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.
Expectation-setting: the protocol tells the reader what to expect, by stating at least one of the following: the expected course or duration of the condition, the signs that should prompt the patient to seek care again or sooner, or what the proposed next step will involve for the patient. Naming an action without any such framing does not satisfy this property.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.
Do not fail this criterion for the absence of pleasantries, empathy statements, or patient-directed formatting. Judge the named behaviors only.
